The id is a lookup into a table; layers then rewrite it.
Context changes the hidden state of the same word.
The network only does arithmetic on numbers.
Final vectors become next-token logits.
Retrieval embeddings are a related but separate object.

questions.q: What happens to a token id at the start of the model?
questions.a: It selects a row of the embedding table — a vector — which then gets a position signal and is rewritten by each layer.

questions.q: Why is 'bank' not a single meaning inside the network?
questions.a: The table row is shared, but hidden states after attention depend on the other tokens (river vs loan).

questions.q: A PM says the model stores a dictionary definition per word. How do you correct them?
questions.a: It stores vectors and computes contextual hidden states. There is no English definition slot.

questions.q: Where do next-token probabilities come from?
questions.a: A linear map from the last-layer vector at the last position to a score per vocab item, then a softmax.

questions.q: Do you need matrix equations to explain this in an interview?
questions.a: No. Id → vector → layers refine with attention → logits. Save the algebra for a research screen.

what-parameter-counts-mean.explain:
## What it is

A **parameter** is a learned number in the model: an entry in a weight matrix or bias. **8B, 70B, 400B+** are counts of those numbers. They measure **capacity** — how much structure the model can represent — not intelligence, not truth, not speed. Most of the count is in the embedding table and the feed-forward layers (or experts, in MoE).

The file on disk is roughly 2 bytes × parameters for 16-bit weights, plus overhead. 70B is a large download and a large GPU memory bill. 8B can run on a single high-end consumer GPU. 400B+ is a cluster.

Count is a size label. It is not a benchmark.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will be asked "should we use the 70B". The count tells you memory and a prior on capacity. It does not tell you quality on your task. Interviewers want the definition and the "not automatically better" that follows in the next item.

They may ask what 8B means in memory (order-of-magnitude: tens of GB in 16-bit, less if quantised). A ballpark is enough.

## How it works + one small example

8B ≈ 8×10^9 numbers. At 2 bytes, ~16 GB of weights, plus KV cache at runtime. 70B ≈ 140 GB at 16-bit — multi-GPU or heavy quantisation. An API hides this; you pay in tokens instead of GPUs.

When a card says 8B, ask: dense or MoE? Active parameters per token may be smaller. When it says 400B, ask: can I even host it, and do I need to?

Use the count to reject impossibilities ("we will self-host 400B on one laptop") not to pick a winner.

## Failure modes

1. **Equating B with quality.**

2. **Forgetting runtime memory** (KV cache) on top of weights.

3. **Ignoring MoE** total vs active.

4. **Treating the API as zero parameters** — you still pay.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Parameters are learned numbers. 8B, 70B, 400B are capacity and memory labels, not a quality ranking. I use the count to know what I can host and what I will pay, then I measure the task.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: A parameter is a learned weight.
- Prove it in an artefact: 8B/70B/400B count those weights.
- Prove it in an artefact: Count ≈ capacity and memory, not truth.
- Prove it in an artefact: Runtime memory also includes the KV cache.
- Prove it in an artefact: MoE: total vs active differ.
- Prove it in an artefact: Use count to reject impossible hosts, not to pick a winner.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Parameters are learned numbers. 8B, 70B, 400B are capacity and memory labels, not a quality ranking. I use the count to know what I can host and what I will pay, then I measure the task.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.q: What does 70B mean?
questions.a: About 70 billion learned numbers in the model. It is a size, not a score.

questions.q: Roughly how much memory are 70B 16-bit weights?
questions.a: On the order of 140 GB for weights alone, plus KV cache. You need multiple GPUs or quantisation.

questions.q: A slide says 'we picked 70B so it is smarter than 8B'. What is missing?
questions.a: An eval on the task, cost, latency, and whether the 8B is specialised. Count is not a ranking.

questions.q: Why does an API user still care about size?
questions.a: It correlates with price and latency, and with which features exist. You do not see the GPUs; you see the bill.

questions.q: Where do most parameters sit?
questions.a: Usually the feed-forward layers (or experts) and the embedding table, not 'the attention idea' as a small object.

why-bigger-is-not-automatically-better.explain:
## What it is

**More parameters can increase capacity** — the model can represent more regularities. **Larger does not automatically mean better** on your task, at your latency, at your price, or under your data constraints. A small model with the right post-training, the right prompt, or the right retrieved context can win. A large model can be slower, more expensive, overconfident, or worse at following a tight schema.

Bigger also means harder to host, harder to eval thoroughly, and easier to assume you can skip engineering. The product question is "better at what".

MoE complicates "bigger": a large total with small active compute is a different bargain.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "just use the biggest" is how invoices die. Interviewers want this sentence verbatim-ish: capacity can go up; quality, cost, and fit may not. They will ask for a counterexample (RAG'd 8B vs naked 70B on internal docs).

This is the practical companion to the parameter-count definition.

## How it works + one small example

Run three rows on 50 real tickets: 8B, 70B, 70B+policy snippet. Report quality, p95, cost. Often the third wins and the first is "good enough". That slide beats a parameter table.

When bigger wins, say so. When it wins by 1% and costs 8×, say that too.

Hosting: if you cannot operate 70B, it is not better *for you*. The API 70B-class model may still be the right buy — that is a path choice, not a parameter religion.

## Failure modes

1. **Sorting the shortlist by B.**

2. **Skipping eval** because the card is impressive.

3. **Ignoring cost × volume.**

4. **Ignoring schema/tool skill** of a smaller tuned model.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

More parameters can mean more capacity. They do not automatically mean better, cheaper, or fitter. I compare models on the task, the latency and the bill. An 8B with the right context often beats a naked 70B.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Capacity ≠ quality on your task.
- Prove it in an artefact: Bigger is slower and dearer unless MoE says otherwise.
- Prove it in an artefact: Context, post-training and tools can beat scale.
- Prove it in an artefact: Hostability is part of 'better'.
- Prove it in an artefact: Always eval.
- Prove it in an artefact: MoE changes what 'bigger' costs to run.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (More parameters can mean more capacity. They do not automatically mean better, cheaper, or fitter. I compare models on the task, the latency and the bill. An 8B with the right context often beats a naked 70B) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

questions.q: Why is bigger not automatically better?
questions.a: Quality is task-specific; cost and latency grow; a smaller specialised or well-prompted model can win. Capacity is only one ingredient.

questions.q: Give a case where an 8B beats a 70B.
questions.a: Internal FAQ with the handbook in context, or a fine-tuned classifier. The 70B without the handbook hallucinates policy.

questions.q: A team upgrades to 70B, quality is flat, invoice is 6×. What did they skip?
questions.a: An eval and a cost model. They bought capacity they did not need.

questions.q: When is bigger the right call?
questions.a: When your eval shows a real quality gap you cannot close with prompt, RAG or tools, and you can pay the latency.

questions.q: How does MoE change this slogan?
questions.a: A model can be 'bigger' in total parameters but cheaper per token if few experts are active. Read both numbers.

the-intuition-behind-attention.explain:
## What it is

**Attention** is the idea that **a token looks at other tokens in the context** to build a better representation of what it means *here*. "Bank" looks at "river" or "loan". A closing brace looks at the opening one. The next-token prediction looks at the instruction and the relevant sentence, not only at the last word.

It is a **weighted mix** of other tokens' vectors. The weights are computed from the current token and the others (how relevant they seem). You do not need the softmax formula in a product interview. You need: every token can draw on the others, and that is why long context is both powerful and expensive.

**Causal** attention (next item) means a token cannot look at the future — only the past and itself.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the one transformer idea you must be able to say in a hallway. Interviewers ask "what is attention" to see if you say "it looks at relevant tokens" or if you freeze. They do not want a paper recitation.

They will ask why long prompts cost more: attention mixes over more pairs (plus the rest of the block). They will ask why order matters (position + causality).

## How it works + one small example

Sentence: "The trophy does not fit in the suitcase because it is too small." Attention is how "it" gathers evidence from "trophy" and "suitcase". A good model puts weight on suitcase for "small".

In a prompt, the last position (where we predict) attends to the instruction, the schema, and the user field that matters. If you bury the instruction, attention may still find it — or it may get lost in the middle (later module).

You cannot turn attention off in a decoder-only LLM. You can write a clearer layout so the relevant tokens are easy to find.

3. **Ignoring causality** — it cannot see future tokens while generating.

4. **Thinking every token is equally mixed.** The weights are selective, but not perfect.

questions.a: A token updates its representation by taking a weighted mix of other tokens in the context.

questions.q: Why does 'bank' mean different things after attention?
questions.a: It mixes in neighbouring tokens like 'river' or 'loan', so the hidden state is contextual.

questions.q: Why are long prompts computationally heavier?

queries-keys-values-causal-attention.explain:
## What it is

At a high level, each token produces three vectors: a **query** ("what am I looking for"), **keys** ("what do I contain"), and **values** ("what I will pass along if you look at me"). Attention scores come from matching queries to keys; the output is a mix of values. A **transformer layer** stacks this (usually in several **heads** that look for different patterns) with a feed-forward rewrite.

**Causal attention** means token t may only look at tokens ≤ t. That is what makes left-to-right generation possible: the model never cheats by seeing the word it is about to predict. Training uses the same mask.

Skip the matrix names in a product interview unless they ask. If they ask, this paragraph is enough.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers sometimes want the Q/K/V words to see if you have read anything past a blog title. They do not want you to derive softmax(QK^T). On the job you will use this when talking about KV cache (the K and V are what we store — next module).

Causal versus bidirectional is why BERT-style encoders differ from GPT-style decoders. Generation is decoder-style.

## How it works + one small example

Predicting the next token at the end of the prompt: that last query looks at all keys in the prompt (and later, in the generated prefix). Values from those positions mix into the last hidden state.

Multi-head: one head might track quotes, another long-range names. You do not configure them.

Causal mask: a triangular mask of "cannot look ahead". If it were bidirectional, generation would not be well-defined in the same way.

KV cache (M1.5): we store keys and values from past tokens so we do not recompute them every step.

## Failure modes

1. **Memorising the formula** and failing the intuition.

2. **Forgetting causal** — "it looks at the whole document including the future".

3. **Confusing heads with experts** (MoE).

4. **Thinking you set Q/K/V** as a user.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Queries ask, keys answer relevance, values are what gets mixed. Layers stack that, causally — a token cannot see the future. That is enough to understand generation and the KV cache. I do not lead with matrix algebra.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Q = what I look for; K = what I offer; V = what I pass along.
- Prove it in an artefact: Scores from Q·K; output is a mix of V.
- Prove it in an artefact: Many heads look for different patterns.
- Prove it in an artefact: Causal: only past and self.
- Prove it in an artefact: KV cache stores K and V from past tokens.
- Prove it in an artefact: Skip the formula unless asked.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Queries ask, keys answer relevance, values are what gets mixed. Layers stack that, causally — a token cannot see the future. That is enough to understand generation and the KV cache. I do not lead with matrix algebra.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

## What it is

A **dense** model uses **every parameter on every token**. Each layer's feed-forward and attention projections run in full. 8B dense means about 8B weights participate in producing the next token (plus the embedding lookup). There is no router and no idle expert.

Dense is the default mental model. It is simple to host: load the weights, run the stack. Memory and compute scale together. If you can fit the weights, you can run the token (KV cache aside).

Most classic GPT-style models you have used are dense unless the card says MoE.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you need the word so you can contrast MoE. Interviewers ask dense versus MoE as a pair. Dense is the simple side: every parameter, every token. They want you to know that 70B dense is expensive to *run*, not only to store.

They may ask why people still train dense (simpler, predictable latency, mature tooling).

## How it works + one small example

Serving: one blob of weights, all used. Latency is relatively stable per token for a given context length. Memory ≈ all weights + KV.

When a card says "7B" and does not mention experts, assume dense. When it says "8x7B" or "total 47B, active 13B", it is MoE.

Product implication: upgrading from 8B dense to 70B dense is a large jump in GPU and token price. Upgrading to an MoE with 13B active may feel closer to 13B at runtime with a larger memory footprint.

1. **Assuming every large model is dense.**

3. **Forgetting KV** when sizing dense memory.

4. **Comparing 70B dense to 70B-total MoE** as equal runtime cost.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Dense means every parameter participates in every token. It is the simple model: memory and compute move together. I assume dense unless the card talks about experts, and I do not compare those costs as equal.

mixture-of-experts-routing.explain:
## What it is

In a **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** transformer, the big **feed-forward** block is replaced by many **experts** (smaller FFNs). A **router** picks **a few** of them for each token — often one or two. Attention usually stays dense. So each token takes a **sparse** path through a **wide** set of specialists.

The router is itself a learned tiny network. It can load-balance badly (all tokens to one expert) if training did not regularise that. You do not set the route as a user.

MoE is why a model can advertise a huge total size and a smaller "active" size.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, cards will say Mixtral-style "8x7B". Interviewers want: many experts, router picks few, compute per token is closer to the active set. They want the catch: you still **store** all experts.

They may ask what the router does if it is wrong (worse quality, uneven load, hot experts).

## How it works + one small example

Picture 8 experts of ~7B FFN each. For token t the router picks expert 2 and 5. Only those FFNs run. Attention still uses all heads. The next token may pick a different pair.

Hosting: the weights of all 8 sit in memory (or are offloaded, slowly). Serving stacks try to place experts across GPUs.

When you read "8x7B" you should ask: 8 experts of what, how many active, and is 7B the expert or the whole dense equivalent. Cards are inconsistent; look for **active parameters**.

## Failure modes

1. **Thinking only one expert exists at a time in memory.**

2. **Thinking you pick the expert** in the API.

3. **Ignoring load imbalance.**

4. **Treating 8x7B as 56B dense compute.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

MoE splits the feed-forward into many experts and a router picks a few per token. Compute stays closer to a smaller model; all experts still have to live in memory. I look for active versus total on the card.

questions.a: A router scores experts for this token and runs only the top few feed-forward experts. Other experts stay idle for that token.

total-vs-active-parameters.explain:
## What it is

**Total parameters** count every weight, including experts that are idle on a given token. **Active parameters** count the weights that **run** for that token (attention + chosen experts + embeddings, depending on the card's definition). An MoE can be **very large in total** and **much cheaper to run** than a dense model of the same total, because FLOPs follow active.

Cards sometimes hide one of the two numbers. "8x7B" is not a standard equation — read the prose. Active is the number that predicts **compute per token**. Total (plus layout) predicts **memory**.

Dense models have total ≈ active.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the interview distinction. If you conflate them you will over-provision GPUs or under-estimate a bill. Interviewers will give a toy: 47B total, 13B active — which number is latency, which is VRAM.

On the job, procurement will quote the bigger number. You ask for both.

## How it works + one small example

Example: Mixtral-class 8×7B is often described as ~47B total and ~13B active. Inference compute feels closer to 13B dense. Memory feels closer to 47B (unless expert offload).

When you size a GPU: start from **total** (or the served precision) for whether it fits. When you size throughput: start from **active** and the serving stack.

When you size an API bill: ignore both and measure tokens — the vendor already folded this in. You still use the distinction to understand *why* two "70B" APIs price differently.

## Failure modes

1. **Using total for FLOPs.**

2. **Using active for VRAM.**

3. **Comparing MoE total to dense total** as equal runtime.

4. **Trusting '8x7B' without the paragraph.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Total is what you store; active is what you run per token. MoE makes them different. I size memory from total and compute from active, and I refuse a slide that shows only one number.

- Prove it in an artefact: Memory follows total; FLOPs follow active.
- Prove it in an artefact: 8x7B is not self-explanatory.
- Prove it in an artefact: API prices already fold this in — still ask why.

what-moe-changes-in-practice.explain:
## What it is

In practice MoE means: **every expert still has to be held in memory** (or paged slowly), while **compute per token stays closer to a much smaller dense model**. You buy a wider brain without paying full dense FLOPs, if the serving stack is good. You pay **engineering**: placement, load balance, tail latency when tokens hit cold experts, and worse batching behaviour than a dense 8B.

Quality is not guaranteed to match a dense model with the same total. It is a different training recipe.

For an API user, MoE may show up as a model name that is "cheap for its quality". You still eval.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the "why is this 47B cheaper than that 70B" conversation. Interviewers want the memory-versus-compute split and one serving wart (load, batching, or offload). They want you not to treat MoE as free lunch.

Self-hosting MoE is a harder ops problem than dense of the active size.

## How it works + one small example

API path: try the MoE id on your eval; look at price and p95. If the vendor hosts it, their ops problem is not yours.

Self-host: you need a stack that understands expert parallelism. A naive "load 47B dense-style" may work but waste. Offloading experts to CPU will crater tokens/s.

Product: MoE is attractive for high-volume, quality-sensitive text where you cannot pay 70B dense. It is less attractive if you need dead-simple single-GPU serving.

Document the model as "MoE, 13B active" in your decision log so the next person does not resize the cluster from the total.

## Failure modes

1. **Free lunch** — ignoring memory and ops.

2. **Offload without measuring** tokens/s.

3. **Expecting dense-like batching.**

4. **Resizing clusters from the total** or from the active blindly.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

MoE keeps all experts in memory and runs only a few per token. I get smaller-model compute with larger-model storage, plus serving complexity. I eval it like any other model and I do not treat it as a free 70B.

- Prove it in an artefact: APIs hide ops; self-host does not.
- Prove it in an artefact: Write 'active vs total' in the decision log.

reading-moe-model-cards.explain:
## What it is

On a card, look for **"8x7B"**, **"n experts"**, **"top-k"**, **"total parameters"**, **"active parameters"**. Those tell you **speed** (active), **cost** (active, plus vendor margin), and **hosting** (total memory, expert layout). Also read context length, licence, and whether the card is for a base or instruct model.

If the card only says a large billions number and "MoE" in a tweet, wait for the two numbers. If the card is a dense model, do not invent experts.

Cards lie by omission. Your eval does not.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers may paste a card snippet and ask what you know about serving. They want you to extract total vs active and say what you still do not know (quality). On the job this is the 10-minute read before you shortlist.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist:

1. Dense or MoE? If MoE: experts, k active, total, active.
2. Precision they measured (bf16 vs 4-bit) — memory changes.
3. Context window and template.
4. Licence (especially open-weight).
5. Benchmarks as a shortlist hint only.

Then: can we host this, or is it API-only for us? If host, which serving stack lists this architecture.

Write one sentence: "47B total / 13B active MoE, instruct, 32k context, Apache-like licence — eval next." That is a card read.

## Failure modes

1. **Stopping at 8x7B.**

2. **Treating card benchmarks as your quality.**

3. **Missing the licence.**

4. **Missing instruct vs base.**

- Prove it in an artefact: Active ≈ speed/cost; total ≈ memory.
- Prove it in an artefact: Precision changes memory.
- Prove it in an artefact: Licence and instruct/base matter.
- Prove it in an artefact: Benchmarks shortlist; they do not ship.
- Prove it in an artefact: One sentence summary, then eval.

They do not tell me quality — that is the eval. residual-streams-and-layer-stacking.explain:
## What it is

Each transformer **block adds a residual update** to a running hidden state (the **residual stream**): `x = x + attention(x)` then `x = x + ffn(x)` (normalisation details vary). **Depth** is how many times you refine that stream. Early layers do more local/syntax-ish work; later layers do more semantic and predictive work — as a rough story, not a law.

The residual connection is why very deep stacks can still train: the original signal can pass through. You do not configure it. You should know that "70 layers" means 70 rounds of refine, not 70 separate models.

This is why people say the representation is refined, not replaced.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers who go slightly deeper than attention will ask what a layer *does* to the vector. "It adds a residual update" is the crisp answer. On the job you will hear "the residual stream" in research-adjacent conversations and in interpretability posts.

You do not need to implement it. You need to not say "each layer overwrites the meaning completely".

## How it works + one small example

Picture a highway of width d. Each block merges in an attention update and an FFN update. The next token's logits read the final highway at the last position.

Skip connections mean a bug or a no-op block does not destroy x. Training is possible at 30–80 layers because of this (plus normalisation).

When someone says "the model is 32 layers", they mean 32 of these blocks stacked. Width (d) and depth (layers) are both capacity, different shapes.

MoE sits inside the FFN update; the residual story is the same.

## Failure modes

1. **Layers as separate models.**

2. **Ignoring residuals** — "each layer starts from scratch".

3. **Over-claiming what early vs late layers do.**

4. **Confusing width and depth.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Each block adds a residual update to a running stream. Depth is how many times we refine that stream, not a stack of separate models. I say 'refine', not 'overwrite'.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: x = x + update, twice per block (attention, FFN).
- Prove it in an artefact: The residual stream is the running hidden state.
- Prove it in an artefact: Depth = stacked refinements.
- Prove it in an artefact: Residuals make deep stacks trainable.
- Prove it in an artefact: Width and depth are different capacity knobs.
- Prove it in an artefact: MoE lives in the FFN update.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Each block adds a residual update to a running stream. Depth is how many times we refine that stream, not a stack of separate models. I say 'refine', not 'overwrite'.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.q: What is a residual stream in a transformer?
questions.a: The running hidden state that each block adds to, rather than replacing. Attention and FFN contribute updates.

questions.q: Why does depth refine a representation?
questions.a: Each block can add information from other tokens (attention) and a nonlinear rewrite (FFN) while keeping the previous signal.

questions.a: One model, one stream, stacked updates. Only the end produces logits.

questions.q: Where does MoE sit in this picture?
questions.a: In the FFN update: the residual add is the same, the update is sparse across experts.

questions.q: Why do residual connections help training?
questions.a: The original signal can pass through. Gradients and information do not have to survive a total rewrite at every layer.

why-positional-information-is-required.explain:
## What it is

Attention, in its raw form, is a **set operation**: without extra information it does not know **order**. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look like the same bag of tokens. **Positional information** — sinusoidal encodings, learned embeddings, RoPE, ALiBi — marks *where* a token sits so the mix can depend on order and distance.

Every production LLM injects position somehow. Context-length limits and "lost in the middle" are partly about how that scheme generalises.

You do not pick a position scheme in the API. You should know why it exists.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers use the dog/man sentence. It is the cleanest test that you understand attention is not enough. On the job you will meet RoPE when a card talks about context extension. You only need the why.

They may ask whether tokens are a sequence or a set — a sequence, because we add position.

## How it works + one small example

Add a position vector (or rotate the Q/K as in RoPE) so the query at position 9 knows it is 9 and can prefer nearby keys.

If you removed position and shuffled training, the model could not learn syntax. We do not do that.

Long-context variants change the position scheme or interpolate it. That is why "we trained at 4k but we run at 128k" is a research claim, not a free lunch — quality may drop.

When you truncate a prompt, you also change positions of what remains. Putting the question last is a layout choice that interacts with position.

## Failure modes

1. **Ignoring order** in the attention story.

2. **Thinking the token id includes position.** It does not.

3. **Assuming infinite context** because RoPE can extrapolate a bit.

4. **Shuffling chunks** in RAG without caring about order.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Without position, attention cannot tell 'dog bites man' from the reverse. We inject positional information so order and distance matter. That is why a sequence is not a bag of words.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Raw attention is permutation-sensitive only after we add position.
- Prove it in an artefact: Dog bites man vs the reverse is the example.
- Prove it in an artefact: RoPE/ALiBi/embeddings are mechanisms; the need is the point.
- Prove it in an artefact: Token id ≠ position.
- Prove it in an artefact: Long-context claims depend on the position scheme.
- Prove it in an artefact: Layout in the prompt interacts with position.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. questions.a: Without it, attention treats tokens as a bag and cannot distinguish 'dog bites man' from the reverse.

questions.q: Does the token id encode where the word sits?
questions.a: No. Position is added separately (embedding, RoPE, etc.). The id is the vocab piece.

questions.a: Order and position change the mix. Also lost-in-the-middle. Use a stable, intentional layout.

questions.q: Why might a model trained at 4k struggle at 128k even if the window 'fits'?
questions.a: The position scheme may not generalise. Longer is not equally usable.

questions.q: Name one positional method you might see on a card.
questions.a: RoPE, ALiBi, or learned absolute embeddings. Knowing why beats naming all of them.

pretraining-self-supervision.explain:
## What it is

**Pretraining** is the long, expensive stage where a model reads a huge text mix and learns to predict the next token. **Self-supervision** means the **label is the next token itself** — no human tagged "this is a noun". Every sequence is a training example. That is how you can spend a trillion tokens without a trillion human labels.

The objective is still next-token prediction. The data is web-scale text, code, books, and whatever the lab mixed. The output of pretraining is a **base model**: a fluent completer, not yet a polite assistant.

You do not run this at work. You consume its result.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will hear "pretrained on internet text" as a privacy and cutoff story. Interviewers want: the signal is the next token; that is self-supervision; that is why scale is possible. They want you to distinguish this from SFT (next topic cluster).

They may ask why the model can write code it was not "taught" as a course — because code was in the mix and the objective does not care about domain.

## How it works + one small example

Take a sentence. Hide the last word. The model predicts it. Slide one token. Repeat. Billions of times. The weights absorb grammar, facts that appeared often, and stylistic priors.

A lab documents the mix at a high level (and often not). You cannot delete a fact from the weights later. You can avoid putting private data into *your* prompts and into any fine-tune you control.

Base checkpoints are what you would continue-pretrain or SFT. Chat products are post-trained descendants.

## Failure modes

1. **Thinking humans labelled every sentence.**

2. **Thinking pretraining is instruction following.**

3. **Thinking you can untrain a fact** with a prompt.

4. **Confusing your RAG corpus with pretraining.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Pretraining is next-token prediction on a huge mix. The label is the next token — self-supervision — which is how you train at that scale. The result is a base completer, not yet a chat assistant.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Pretraining: predict the next token on a huge mix.
- Prove it in an artefact: Self-supervision: the next token is the label.
- Prove it in an artefact: No human tag per sentence.
- Prove it in an artefact: Output is a base model, not an assistant.
- Prove it in an artefact: You consume this; you do not run it at work.
- Prove it in an artefact: Facts in the mix are not a database you can edit.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Pretraining is next-token prediction on a huge mix. The label is the next token — self-supervision — which is how you train at that scale. The result is a base completer, not yet a chat assistant. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

questions.q: What is self-supervised about pretraining?
questions.a: The next token in the text is the label. You do not need a human to tag each example.

questions.q: Why can labs train on trillions of tokens?
questions.a: Every sequence yields many next-token examples. The web and code dumps scale; human labels do not.

questions.q: A PM says the model was taught tickets like a course. What actually happened?
questions.a: If tickets were not in the mix, it was not taught. Fluency on support-like prose is transfer from similar text, not your schema.

questions.q: What do you get at the end of pretraining?
questions.a: A base model that completes text. Instruction following comes later.

questions.q: Can you delete a pretrained fact with a system prompt?
questions.a: You can steer away from it; you cannot erase the weights. For private facts, do not put them in training you control, and do not rely on prompts as deletion.

what-pretraining-teaches.explain:
## What it is

From next-token prediction on a huge mix the model picks up **grammar**, **frequent facts**, **patterns**, **concepts**, **relationships**, **code syntax**, and **problem-solving patterns** that were written down often enough. It is a statistical imprint, not a curriculum. Rare facts and private facts are missing or fragile. Skills that were never in text (your internal tool API) are absent.

"Teaches" is a metaphor. The objective never said "learn grammar". Grammar is useful for predicting the next token, so it appears.

This is why a base model can complete a Python function and also complete a toxic rant — both were in the mix.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers ask what pretraining gives you so they can ask what it does *not*. On the job this is why you still need SFT, tools, and RAG. A candidate who thinks pretraining = a helpful employee has skipped post-training.

This also explains surprising transfer: math word problems in the mix help some reasoning; Stack Overflow helps code.

## How it works + one small example

Evidence you will see: a base model continues `def fib(n):` with plausible code. It continues `The CEO of` with a likely name that may be stale. It continues an unfinished insult.

What it did not learn: your ticket schema, last week's price, the decision to refuse harm. Those are post-training, tools, or context.

When a capability appears "for free" (JSON-ish, HTML), it is usually because those strings were common. When it fails (your proprietary DSL), you add examples or a grammar.

## Failure modes

1. **Curriculum story** — someone sat and taught topics.

2. **Assuming rare facts are solid.**

3. **Assuming ethics were in the objective.**

4. **Expecting private APIs** to be known.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Pretraining imprints grammar, common facts, code syntax and patterns that helped predict the next token. It is not a course and it is not your company handbook. Rare, private and post-cutoff things are missing.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Grammar, frequent facts, patterns, code syntax emerge from the objective.
- Prove it in an artefact: There is no topic curriculum.
- Prove it in an artefact: Rare and private facts are weak or absent.
- Prove it in an artefact: Base models complete; they do not politely refuse by design.
- Prove it in an artefact: Transfer comes from similar text in the mix.
- Prove it in an artefact: Your DSL and schema are not in there.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Pretraining imprints grammar, common facts, code syntax and patterns that helped predict the next token. It is not a course and it is not your company handbook. Rare, private and post-cutoff things are missing) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

There is no topic curriculum.
Rare and private facts are weak or absent.
Base models complete; they do not politely refuse by design.

Your DSL and schema are not in there.

questions.q: What kinds of things does pretraining tend to imprint?
questions.a: Grammar, common facts, regular patterns, relationships, code syntax, and problem formats that appeared often.

questions.q: Why can a base model write Python but not your internal RPC DSL?
questions.a: Python is all over the mix. Your DSL is not. You add examples, a grammar, or a tool.

questions.q: A base model completes a hateful prompt fluently. Is pretraining broken?
questions.a: No. That text was in the mix and the objective is completion. Refusal is post-training.

questions.q: Where do 'skills' like JSON shape come from?
questions.a: Lots of JSON in the mix, plus later SFT. Not a JSON module you can toggle.

questions.q: Did anyone label 'this sentence teaches grammar'?
questions.a: No. Grammar helped predict tokens, so the weights reflect it.

memorization-vs-generalization.explain:
## What it is

**Memorisation** is reproducing a training string (or a near copy). **Generalisation** is producing a useful continuation for a prompt the model has **never seen verbatim**. LLMs do both. A famous paragraph may come back almost intact. A new ticket subject line still gets a plausible label because similar patterns existed.

You cannot tell from one fluent answer which happened. That is why "it knew the answer" is not evidence of a lookup, and why copyright and privacy teams care about extraction attacks.

Generalisation is why few-shot works. Memorisation is why data leaks and eval contamination exist.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers ask how a model can answer a question it has not seen — pattern completion, not a new brain. They ask whether models memorise — yes, especially duplicated or unique strings. On the job this is eval contamination (M1.11) and "don't put secrets in training".

The senior line: we assume both, we measure on held-out real tasks, we do not put secrets in any corpus we control.

## How it works + one small example

Near-copy: a Wikipedia opening line might be regenerated. That can be memorisation.

New combo: "Classify this ticket about a 2026 promo code the model never saw" — if it says billing, that is generalisation from other promo-code tickets in the mix or in context.

You test generalisation with **your** held-out examples, not with MMLU items that may have leaked. You reduce memorisation risk by not training on passwords, and by not needing the model to be the store of unique text.

If legal asks "can it regurgitate our book", the honest answer is "possibly if it was in the mix or the prompt; we will not put the book in a fine-tune without review".

## Failure modes

1. **All answers are memorised.** Then few-shot would not work.

2. **Nothing is memorised.** Then extraction and contamination would not exist.

3. **Using public bench items as proof of generalisation.**

4. **Training on secrets.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Models both memorise and generalise. A new ticket can still be labelled; a famous paragraph can come back. I do not treat fluency as lookup, I eval on held-out real work, and I keep secrets out of any corpus I control.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Memorisation: near-copy of training text.
- Prove it in an artefact: Generalisation: useful output on unseen prompts.
- Prove it in an artefact: Models do both; fluency does not tell you which.
- Prove it in an artefact: Few-shot relies on generalisation.
- Prove it in an artefact: Contamination and leaks rely on memorisation.
- Prove it in an artefact: Held-out real tasks measure the thing you care about.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Models both memorise and generalise. A new ticket can still be labelled; a famous paragraph can come back. I do not treat fluency as lookup, I eval on held-out real work, and I keep secrets out of any corpus I control.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.q: How can a model answer a question it has not seen verbatim?
questions.a: It generalises patterns from similar text. That is not a stored Q&A card, and it is not proof of truth.

questions.q: When should you worry about memorisation?
questions.a: When unique or sensitive strings were in training, when you use public benches, or when legal asks about regurgitation.

questions.q: A demo uses an MMLU question the model nails. Why is that weak evidence?
questions.a: The item may have been in the mix (contamination). Use a private held-out set.

questions.q: Where do you put a customer password?
questions.a: Never in pretraining, fine-tunes, logs, or prompts if you can avoid it. The model is not a vault, and it can memorise.

questions.q: Is a correct label on a new ticket memorisation?
questions.a: Usually generalisation (or context). You cannot be sure from one example; that is why you measure on many held-out tickets.

the-post-training-pipeline.explain:
## What it is

The usual pipeline is **Pretraining → Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) → Preference / Reinforcement training → Deployed assistant**. Pretraining makes a completer. **SFT** teaches it to follow example dialogues (helpful format). **Preference** training (RLHF, DPO, RLAIF, …) teaches it which of two answers people (or a judge model) prefer. **Safety** tuning is mixed through these stages. The thing you call in a chat API is the end of this pipe, not the base checkpoint.

Labs vary the names and skip or repeat stages. The idea is stable: first predict the internet, then imitate assistants, then rank better answers.

You can stop after SFT and ship a cheaper, narrower model. Many "instruct" open weights are mostly SFT.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask you to name the pipe in order. On the job this is why a base model feels rude and a chat model hedges. It is also why "fine-tune" in a meeting is ambiguous — SFT or preference?

If you cannot order the stages you will mis-buy a base model for a chatbot.

## How it works + one small example

Story: base completes `User: How do I reset my password?` with more forum junk. After SFT it produces an assistant-shaped reply. After preference it prefers the reply that does not leak another user's reset link and that asks for the account email in the right tone.

Your job: pick the right checkpoint (base vs instruct vs "reasoning"), and if you fine-tune, know which stage you are imitating. Do not RLHF in the first week of a product.

Document the pipeline on a slide with four boxes. That slide earns trust.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling a base model** in a chat product.

2. **Saying RLHF is pretraining.**

3. **Fine-tuning away safety** by accident with a sloppy SFT set.

4. **Skipping SFT** and hoping preference magically adds format.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Pretrain, then SFT, then preference, then the assistant you call. Base completes the internet; SFT teaches the format; preference teaches taste. I name the stage I am buying or changing.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Order: pretrain → SFT → preference → deploy.
- Prove it in an artefact: Base ≠ chat.
- Prove it in an artefact: SFT imitates dialogues; preference ranks them.
- Prove it in an artefact: Safety is woven through, not a separate magic box.

sft-rlhf-preference-optimization.explain:
## What it is

**SFT** is supervised learning on **prompt → ideal response** pairs. The model imitates the target tokens. **RLHF** uses a **reward model** trained on human comparisons, then updates the policy to score higher (classic PPO-style). **RLAIF** uses an AI judge instead of (or with) humans. **Preference optimisation** (DPO and friends) skips an explicit RL loop and trains directly on preferred vs rejected pairs. **Safety tuning** is extra data and constraints in these stages so the model refuses or redirects certain requests.

All of these are **conceptual** for this level: they change what completions are likely, they do not give you a truth layer.

Labs mix them. You rarely implement PPO at work; you might SFT.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask SFT vs RLHF in one minute (there is a dedicated interview item). They want: SFT = imitate format; preference = pick the better of two. On the job, when a vendor says "aligned", this is the bag of methods they might mean.

They may ask why noisy raters matter (next item but one).

## How it works + one small example

SFT example: 5_000 tickets with the reply you wish agents sent. The model learns that shape.

Preference example: for the same ticket, reply A (empathetic, correct policy) vs B (refunds everything). Humans or a judge pick A. The model becomes more A-like.

Safety: pairs that refuse bomb-making and still help with chemistry homework. Imperfect.

If you SFT on sloppy answers, you imitate slop. If you preference-train on raters who love long answers, you get verbose models. Data quality is the product.

## Failure modes

1. **SFT on unreviewed dumps.**

2. **Preference without a rubric** — raters pick style, not truth.

3. **Calling every method RLHF.**

4. **Expecting safety to be absolute.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

SFT imitates ideal replies. Preference training (RLHF, DPO, RLAIF) pushes toward the answer raters like better. Safety is extra data in those stages. None of them is a truth oracle; the pairs are the product.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: SFT: imitate prompt→response pairs.
- Prove it in an artefact: RLHF: reward model + policy update.
- Prove it in an artefact: DPO-like: learn from preferred vs rejected directly.
- Prove it in an artefact: RLAIF: AI judges instead of or with humans.
- Prove it in an artefact: Safety is data and constraints, not a lock.
- Prove it in an artefact: The pairs decide the personality.

why-chat-models-behave-as-they-do.explain:
## What it is

Chat models **follow instructions**, **answer conversationally**, **refuse** some requests, **hedge**, **structure** answers, and **ask for clarification** because **post-training rewarded those behaviours**, not because the transformer grew a conscience. Base models do not naturally do this. If your SFT set is terse tables, the chat model will be terse. If preference raters like "as an AI language model" hedges, you get hedges.

Refusals are incomplete. A determined user can often jailbreak a tendency. That is why product safety is still policy + tools + filters.

When a model is "helpful" it is imitating helpfulness in the data.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers ask why ChatGPT-style models talk as they do. The answer is post-training. On the job this explains a vendor change: they updated preference data and now the tone shifted. It also explains why your SFT can overwrite the niceness you liked — or the refusals you needed.

Do not moralise the model. Design around tendencies.

## How it works + one small example

Observe: the same base family, two post-trains, two personalities. One refuses medical advice; one gives a structured disclaimer plus general info. That is data.

If you need a model that always asks one clarifying question when the ticket is empty, put that in SFT and test it. Do not rely on generic helpfulness.

If you need a refusal, also enforce it in code for the actions that matter (no refund tool without a reason code).

When behaviour drifts after a provider update, re-run the golden set; do not argue with the blog.

## Failure modes

1. **Attributing tone to 'the architecture'.**

2. **Relying on refusal** as a security control.

3. **SFT that accidentally removes hedges** you legally wanted — or adds them everywhere.

4. **Not re-evaling** after a vendor post-train.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Chat behaviour is post-trained: instructions, tone, refusals, hedges, structure. It is imitation and preference, not a soul. I encode the behaviour I need in data and tests, and I enforce actions in code.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Instruction following is taught after pretraining.
- Prove it in an artefact: Tone, refuse, hedge, structure come from SFT and preference.
- Prove it in an artefact: Base models complete; they do not chat by default.
- Prove it in an artefact: Refusals are tendencies, not locks.
- Prove it in an artefact: Your SFT set is a personality.
- Prove it in an artefact: Re-eval after vendor post-train updates.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Chat behaviour is post-trained: instructions, tone, refusals, hedges, structure. It is imitation and preference, not a soul. I encode the behaviour I need in data and tests, and I enforce actions in code.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.a: Your pairs did not include those refusals (or contradicted them). You overwrote a post-train behaviour. Add the cases or keep a separate policy layer.

questions.a: No. It is a trained tendency. Enforce dangerous actions in tools and application code.

questions.a: They changed post-training data or mix. Your prompts sit on a new personality. Re-run evals.

instruction-following-is-post-trained.explain:
## What it is

**Base models complete text.** If you start a sentence they finish it. **Chat behaviour is taught after pretraining** with SFT and preference. "Instruction following" is not an emergent switch that flips at 70B; it is a **post-trained skill**. That is why you must pick an instruct checkpoint, apply the chat template, and not send chat-formatted traffic to a base model.

A base model can still follow an instruction if the completion looks like the web (a tutorial that continues with the answer). It is unreliable. Products use instruct models.

This is the one-line version of the pipeline, worth its own card.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

People download a base Llama and then say "open models are dumb". They skipped post-training and the template. Interviewers will trap you with that. On the job, the model picker must show base vs instruct.

Hiring screens: "what's the difference between llama-base and llama-instruct" — this topic.

## How it works + one small example

Wrong: send `[INST] ... [/INST]` to a base model, or send raw "Q: ... A:" to a chat model with the wrong template.

Right: instruct model + official template. If you only have a base model, you are doing research or you are about to SFT.

When a vendor offers `*-base` and `*-instruct`, the second is the product default. The first is for fine-tuning or completion.

Test: give a one-line instruction with no few-shot. Base drifts; instruct usually answers in assistant style.

## Failure modes

1. **Base model in a chatbot.**

2. **Blaming the family** when you used the wrong checkpoint.

3. **Wrong template** on an instruct model (looks like base-level quality).

4. **Assuming scale = instruction following.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Base models complete; instruction following is post-trained. I call an instruct checkpoint with its chat template. If I pick base by mistake I should not blame the family.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Base = completer. Instruct = post-trained follower.
- Prove it in an artefact: Instruction following is taught, not a size unlock.
- Prove it in an artefact: Use the matching chat template.
- Prove it in an artefact: Base in a chatbot is a mispick.
- Prove it in an artefact: You SFT base (or continue from instruct) on purpose.
- Prove it in an artefact: Wrong template looks like a dumb model.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Base models complete; instruction following is post-trained. I call an instruct checkpoint with its chat template. If I pick base by mistake I should not blame the family) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

questions.a: Base completes internet-like text. Instruct was SFT/preference-trained to follow chat instructions.

questions.a: Did you take the instruct checkpoint and apply its chat template? If you used base, switch.

preference-data-quality-beats-volume.explain:
## What it is

**Noisy raters teach the wrong taste.** A million sloppy comparisons lose to ten thousand careful ones with a rubric. Preference data has **label error**, **position bias**, **sycophancy** (raters like agreeableness), and **verbosity bias**. Volume without a rubric scales the bias.

This is true of SFT gold too, but preference is worse because the signal is a pairwise click, not a full target string.

Labs spend a lot on rater guidelines for this reason. Your internal "thumbs" button is the same problem if PMs click without a definition of good.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a thumbs-down stream is not an RLHF dataset. Interviewers want to hear that you would write a rubric and spot-check raters (or a judge). They want "quality beats volume" as a sentence.

This also explains sycophantic products: users upvote agreement.

## How it works + one small example

If you collect preferences: write a rubric (correct, cited, safe, concise). Double-rate a sample. Drop rater pairs that disagree too often. Balance length. Blind the order.

If you use an AI judge, eval the judge against a human gold set. A cheap judge with 20% error will train a cheap personality.

For a product, start with SFT on a small gold set you trust. Add preference only when you can afford the rubric. Do not dump six months of thumbs into DPO on a Friday.

## Failure modes

1. **Thumbs as ground truth.**

2. **No rubric.**

3. **Judge model unchecked.**

4. **More data to fix a biased process** — you get more bias.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Preference quality beats volume. Noisy raters and unchecked judges teach the wrong taste — verbosity, sycophancy, style over truth. I write a rubric, I spot-check, and I will not DPO on raw thumbs.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Pairwise clicks are easy to get wrong.
- Prove it in an artefact: Biases: length, position, sycophancy, style.
- Prove it in an artefact: A rubric and double-rating beat a million noisy pairs.
- Prove it in an artefact: AI judges need their own eval.
- Prove it in an artefact: Product thumbs ≠ RLHF dataset.
- Prove it in an artefact: Volume scales bias if the process is biased.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Preference quality beats volume. Noisy raters and unchecked judges teach the wrong taste — verbosity, sycophancy, style over truth. I write a rubric, I spot-check, and I will not DPO on raw thumbs. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

questions.a: If raters are noisy or biased, you are amplifying the wrong taste. Quality of pairs beats volume.

questions.q: What would you put in a rater rubric for support replies?
questions.a: Correct policy, no invented refunds, no leaked PII, concise, next step clear. Not 'sounds nice' alone.

questions.a: A click between two answers carries less information than a full target string, and raters disagree.

what-happens-after-you-send-a-prompt.explain:
## What it is

After you send a prompt the server **tokenises** it, **runs the model on the input** (prefill), then **predicts a token**, **emits it**, and **repeats** until a stop or a limit. The HTTP response may be **streamed** (tokens as they appear) or buffered. Your client sees text. Underneath it is the same predict → choose → append loop.

There is no separate "thinking" unless the product added a reasoning stage (M1.7). There is no session: the next call must resend history if you want memory.

Errors (rate limit, context overflow, timeout) happen at this boundary, not inside a soul.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the mental model for timeouts and partial streams. Interviewers want the loop after the API call, not only "it generates". They want you to mention tokenise, prefill, decode, stop.

This is the umbrella; the next items split prefill vs decode and the latency metrics.

## How it works + one small example

Client: POST messages. Server: apply template → ids → prefill → for i in max_tokens: decode one, stream it, stop on EOS. Return usage counts.

If you stream, the user sees early tokens while decode continues. If you buffer, TTFT is hidden until the full string exists — usually worse UX for long answers.

If the prompt is too long, you fail before the first token. If decode is slow, you have a first token and then a trickle.

Log request id, token counts, and whether you hit stop or length.

## Failure modes

1. **Thinking the server stored the chat.**

2. **Ignoring tokenisation** as a step (wrong template).

3. **Buffering a long answer** and calling the API 'slow' when it was your wait.

4. **No stop**, hitting max every time.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The API tokenises, prefills the prompt, then decodes tokens until stop. I stream when the user is waiting, I resend history if I want memory, and I log tokens and the stop reason.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Tokenise → prefill → decode loop → stop.
- Prove it in an artefact: Streaming shows tokens as they are chosen.
- Prove it in an artefact: No session unless you resend history.
- Prove it in an artefact: Context overflow fails before useful output.
- Prove it in an artefact: Usage counts are the bill.
- Prove it in an artefact: Reasoning, if any, is an extra stage some products add.

questions.a: The API is stateless. You must resend history (or a summary) each call.

prefill-vs-decode.explain:
## What it is

**Prefill** is the pass (or passes) that **process the whole input** so every prompt token has keys/values and the last position can predict the first output token. It is **compute-heavy** and **parallel** over the input length. **Decode** is **one new token at a time**, using the KV cache, mostly **memory-bandwidth** bound. They have different scaling: prefill grows with **input** length; decode grows with **output** length.

A huge prompt and a one-word answer: you pay prefill. A tiny prompt and a novel: you pay decode. Reasoning models add more decode (or a hidden decode) before the user-visible answer.

This split is the most useful inference idea in interviews.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "the model is slow" is either TTFT (prefill) or tokens/s (decode). The fix differs: shrink the prompt vs cap the output or pick a faster decoder. Interviewers will ask you to define both and to say which one a 50-page context hurts (prefill, and memory).

They will ask why batching helps one more than the other (later item).

## How it works + one small example

Measure TTFT and time-per-output-token separately. If TTFT grows linearly with prompt size, you are seeing prefill. If a 2_000-token answer crawls after a quick first token, you are seeing decode.

Engineering: cache a stable prefix (vendor prompt cache) to skip repeated prefill. Stream decode. Do not stuff a PDF if a paragraph will do.

When you add RAG, you grow prefill. When you ask for "be thorough", you grow decode. Both are money.

## Failure modes

1. **One 'latency' number** that hides which phase.

2. **Shrinking output** when the pain is a 100k prompt.

3. **Pasting books** and blaming the GPU brand.

4. **Ignoring that reasoning is extra decode.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prefill processes the input and sets TTFT; decode emits tokens one by one. I measure them separately. Long prompts hurt prefill; long answers hurt decode. The fixes are different.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Prefill: whole input, parallel, compute-heavy, sets first token.
- Prove it in an artefact: Decode: one token at a time, often memory-bound.
- Prove it in an artefact: Input length → prefill. Output length → decode.
- Prove it in an artefact: Measure TTFT and time per token separately.
- Prove it in an artefact: Prompt cache attacks repeated prefill.
- Prove it in an artefact: Reasoning adds decode you may not see.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Prefill processes the input and sets TTFT; decode emits tokens one by one. I measure them separately. Long prompts hurt prefill; long answers hurt decode. The fixes are different.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.q: What is prefill versus decode?
questions.a: Prefill processes the prompt so the first output token can be predicted. Decode generates each later token sequentially using cached keys/values.

questions.q: A 40-page prompt and a one-word answer feels slow. Which phase?
questions.a: Prefill (and memory). Shrink or cache the prompt. Decode is tiny.

questions.q: TTFT is fine but the essay takes forever. Which phase?
questions.a: Decode. Cap tokens, ask for shorter answers, or pick a higher tokens/s model.

questions.q: How does a prompt cache help?
questions.a: It reuses the prefill work (K/V) for a stable prefix so repeated calls skip that compute.

questions.q: Why is decode hard to parallelise across tokens?
questions.a: Token t+1 depends on token t. You can batch many requests, not future tokens of the same request (except speculative tricks).

tokens-ttft-total-latency.explain:
## What it is

**Input tokens** are the prompt (plus template, tools, history). **Output tokens** are the completion (plus hidden thinking if billed). **TTFT** is time to first token — mostly **prefill** plus queueing. **Tokens per second** is decode throughput. **Total latency** is TTFT + (output tokens / tokens per second), plus network.

A user staring at a blank box cares about TTFT. A batch job cares about total. A stream can feel fast with mediocre total if tokens start early.

Queueing is part of TTFT in a busy API. Your local benchmark may hide it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job these are the SLA words. Interviewers will ask you to define them and to estimate: 800 input, 200 output, 50 ms/token decode, 1.2 s TTFT → about 1.2 + 10 s. They want the formula, not a vibe.

They will ask which number to put on a dashboard (all of them, plus error rate).

## How it works + one small example

Instrument every call:

```
ttft = first_token_time - send_time
tps = (n_out - 1) / (end - first_token_time)
total = end - send_time
```

Alert on TTFT (prefill regressions, queue) and on tps (decode regressions) separately. Cap `max_tokens` so total cannot explode.

When comparing models, do not compare total only: a verbose model looks slower even at the same tps.

For interactive chat, optimise TTFT first. For summarising a book, optimise tokens/s and consider a smaller model.

## Failure modes

1. **One latency metric.**

2. **Forgetting queue time.**

3. **Comparing totals with different output lengths.**

4. **No max_tokens.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Input and output tokens, TTFT, tokens/s, total. Total ≈ TTFT + output/tps. I dashboard them separately because the fixes differ, and I cap output so total cannot run away.
