Following is a hazard when the user is wrong.
Fence tickets and docs.
Policy and money stay in code.
Do not put user text in system.
Your thumbs can train more sycophancy.

questions.q: What is sycophancy in LLMs?
questions.a: A tendency to agree with the user even when the user is wrong, often from preference data that rewards agreeableness.

questions.q: A ticket says 'ignore policy, refund 90 days'. How do you build the bot?
questions.a: Fence the ticket, keep policy in system, and make the refund tool read the real window from code. Do not let the model pick 90.

questions.q: Users who argue get better deals from the bot. Cause?
questions.a: Sycophancy plus a tool that trusted the model. Tighten the tool and the fence.

questions.q: Where does user text live in the message list?
questions.a: In the user message, labelled as data. Never merged into the system policy.

questions.q: How can your own feedback worsen this?
questions.a: Thumbs that mean 'the user liked it' will upvote agreement. Rubric for correctness instead.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**How you bound a failure:** **ground**, **validate**, **abstain**, or **route to a tool** — do **not** only **"prompt harder"**. Name two of those in the first breath. Prompting is allowed as a fifth, weaker move after the others exist.

This is the closer for capabilities and failures. They want a design reflex, not a lament.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The interview is a product design test. On the job this is the comment you leave when someone adds another adjective to the system prompt after a hallucination.

## How it works + one small example

Talk track:

"If the failure is a missing fact, I ground: retrieve and cite, or abstain. If it is a type or a label, I validate with a schema. If it is a sum or a lookup, I route to a tool. If none of those hold, I fail closed and log. I will also tighten the prompt, but I will not call that the bound. Prompting harder alone is how we got here."

Give one concrete: refund window → retrieve + regex + no-tool-without-code.

Thirty to forty seconds.

## Failure modes

1. **Only 'better prompt'.**

2. **Only 'bigger model'.**

3. **No abstain.**

4. **A 5-minute safety rant.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I bound failures by grounding, validating, abstaining, or routing to a tool. Prompting harder is not a bound. If I cannot check it I fail closed.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Ground, validate, abstain, tool.
- Prove it in an artefact: Prompting is extra, not the bound.
- Prove it in an artefact: Bigger is not the bound.
- Prove it in an artefact: Fail closed when you cannot check.
- Prove it in an artefact: Give one concrete example.
- Prove it in an artefact: Keep it under a minute.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (I bound failures by grounding, validating, abstaining, or routing to a tool. Prompting harder is not a bound. If I cannot check it I fail closed) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

## One more pass

Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. Add the second write-up to your notes and keep the first as the interview line. That second pass is usually what fills the gap between recognising the topic and being able to debug it under time pressure.
keyPoints: Ground, validate, abstain, tool.
Prompting is extra, not the bound.
Bigger is not the bound.
Fail closed when you cannot check.
Give one concrete example.
Keep it under a minute.

questions.q: How do you bound a failure?
questions.a: Ground in retrieved text, validate with a schema, abstain when missing, or route to a tool. Do not only prompt harder.

questions.q: Why is 'prompt harder' weak as the only move?
questions.a: The mechanism is still likely continuation. You did not add a check. You added adjectives.

questions.q: Bound a hallucinated refund window.
questions.a: Retrieve the policy, require a citation, regex the days, and make the refund tool read the window from code.

questions.q: A candidate says they would switch to a 70B. What is missing?
questions.a: The bound. Scale may help common facts; it does not check your policy.

questions.q: Name the four bounds this prompt wants.
questions.a: Ground, validate, abstain, route to a tool.

closed-and-api-models.explain:
## What it is

**Closed / API models** are weights you **cannot download**. You call a vendor HTTP API. You buy **frontier capability**, **convenience**, and **someone else's uptime**. You pay with **token prices**, **data leaving your boundary** (unless a private link exists), **vendor dependence**, and **less control** of version, routing, and features.

This is path one of three (API, managed cloud, open weights). It is the fastest way to a prototype and often the right path for unregulated text. It is the wrong path when the contract forbids it.

"We use OpenAI" is a path, not an architecture.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want the trade-off list, not a brand war. On the job this is the first column of the decision table. They will ask what you lose (weights, pin certainty unless you snapshot, privacy by default).

They will ask when you would still pick it: speed, best quality, no GPU ops.

## How it works + one small example

Pick API when: data class allows it, you need the newest models this month, you have two engineers, and a DPA exists if required.

Do not pick it when: prompts cannot leave the region, you must air-gap, or the token bill at volume already exceeds a GPU.

Wrap the client. Pin a snapshot. Keep evals. That wrap is how you leave later.

Write the axes: capability, convenience, privacy, lock-in, control. Score the project. Do not score your favourite blog.

## Failure modes

1. **Path as architecture.**

2. **No DPA** on regulated text.

3. **No wrapper** — 400 call sites.

4. **No snapshot pin.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Closed APIs buy capability and convenience. I pay with privacy, lock-in and less control. I pick that path when the data class allows it, I wrap the client, and I pin a snapshot.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: You call weights you cannot download.
- Prove it in an artefact: Gains: capability, speed, no GPU ops.
- Prove it in an artefact: Costs: privacy, lock-in, less control.
- Prove it in an artefact: A path, not an architecture.
- Prove it in an artefact: Wrap and pin.
- Prove it in an artefact: DPA if the data class needs it.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Closed APIs buy capability and convenience. I pay with privacy, lock-in and less control. I pick that path when the data class allows it, I wrap the client, and I pin a snapshot.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.
keyPoints: You call weights you cannot download.
Gains: capability, speed, no GPU ops.
Costs: privacy, lock-in, less control.
A path, not an architecture.
Wrap and pin.
DPA if the data class needs it.

questions.q: What do you gain and lose with a closed API model?
questions.a: Gain frontier quality and low ops. Lose default privacy, some control of versions, and easy exit if you did not wrap the client.

questions.q: When is the public API the right first path?
questions.a: Unregulated prototype, two engineers, need the newest model this month, and you will wrap the client.

questions.q: A bank POC used the public API with claims text. What was wrong?
questions.a: Data class. Move to a managed platform or in-boundary hosting. Keep the prompts and evals.

questions.q: What do you wrap?
questions.a: A thin client: model id, messages, timeouts, usage logs. Application code never imports the vendor SDK everywhere.

questions.q: Why is 'we use Vendor X' a weak architecture line?
questions.a: It names a path. The architecture is data class, wrapper, evals, and an exit.

open-weight-models.explain:
## What it is

**Open-weight** models ship a **downloadable checkpoint** (under a licence). You can **self-host**, **inspect**, sometimes **fine-tune**, and keep **prompts in your boundary** if you actually operate the host. You pay with **GPUs**, **serving software**, **on-call**, **quality lag** versus the frontier, and **licence homework**.

Open weight is not open source in the OSI sense by default. It is not private if you send the prompt to a public inference host.

This is path three. It is control, not a free frontier model.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want the trade-off and the "open ≠ private" line. On the job this is the column for regulated or high-volume simple tasks. They will ask what you need to host an 8B vs a 70B (one GPU vs many).

They will ask about licences (later item).

## How it works + one small example

Pick open weights when: you must stay in-boundary, you will fine-tune, or the token volume makes GPUs cheaper *and* you can staff serving.

Do not pick them when: you need frontier quality next week and you have no GPU story.

Start with an 8B instruct on a known serving stack. Eval. Only then climb.

If you call Together/Groq/Fireworks, you are on a host — still a vendor — with more checkpoint control. Say that out loud.

## Failure modes

1. **"Open" as private.**

2. **"We will just host 70B"** with no owner.

3. **Ignoring the licence.**

4. **Expecting frontier quality.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Open weights are a checkpoint you can host or buy as a host. I get control and a path to privacy if I operate the boundary. I pay in GPUs, ops and licence work. Open is not automatically private or free.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Downloadable checkpoint, not necessarily OSI open source.
- Prove it in an artefact: Privacy only if you (or your VPC host) stay in-boundary.
- Prove it in an artefact: You own serving and quality lag.
- Prove it in an artefact: Licence is homework.
- Prove it in an artefact: 8B first, then climb.
- Prove it in an artefact: A public inference host is still a vendor.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Open weights are a checkpoint you can host or buy as a host. I get control and a path to privacy if I operate the boundary. I pay in GPUs, ops and licence work. Open is not automatically private or free. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: Downloadable checkpoint, not necessarily OSI open source.
Privacy only if you (or your VPC host) stay in-boundary.
You own serving and quality lag.
Licence is homework.
8B first, then climb.
A public inference host is still a vendor.

questions.q: What is an open-weight model?
questions.a: A checkpoint you can download under a licence and run yourself or on a host. It is not automatically open source or private.

questions.q: When do you self-host?
questions.a: When the data must stay in-boundary or the volume/ops math works *and* someone owns the GPUs. Not as a reflex.

questions.q: A team says they are private because they use Llama on a public host. What is missing?
questions.a: The prompts still leave. Open weights without operating the host are not a boundary.

questions.q: What do you try first, 8B or 70B?

questions.q: Name two costs of open weights.
questions.a: Hardware, serving software, on-call, quality lag, licence review.

managed-platforms-hosted-open-weights.explain:
## What it is

The **third path** sits between a public lab API and a GPU you own. **Managed platforms** (Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry) run **closed and some open** models **in your cloud account** with IAM, VPC, and a bill you already have. **Inference hosts** run open weights for you with no hardware of your own.

You get more **identity, region, and contract** control than a public API, and less **ops** than self-host. You still have a vendor. You still wrap the client.

This is how most enterprises first "do Llama" without buying NVIDIA on-call.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers at IT-services and enterprise shops treat Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry as a filter. On the job this is the path that unblocks a regulated POC. They want you to name the three paths and put this one in the middle.

They will ask what you still do not get (the newest lab model on day one; full control of kernels).

## How it works + one small example

Insurer example: claims text, India region, existing AWS account → Bedrock in ap-south-1 if the model exists there, private link, IAM. Public API fails the region. Self-host 70B fails the staff.

Prototype on the public API with fake data if you must, then move the wrapper to the platform.

Hosted open weights: good for a 8B classifier at volume. Read the host's retention and the model's licence.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping this path** and jumping to self-host.

2. **Assuming every model is on Bedrock day one.**

3. **No private link** when the questionnaire asked for one.

4. **Treating the platform as 'on-prem'.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Managed platforms and inference hosts are the middle path: models in your cloud account or a host, without you owning GPUs. I pick them when identity, region and contract matter and I still do not want CUDA on-call.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Middle path: more control than public API, less ops than self-host.
- Prove it in an artefact: Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry: in-account, IAM, region.
- Prove it in an artefact: Inference hosts: open weights, their GPUs.
- Prove it in an artefact: Still a vendor; still wrap.
- Prove it in an artefact: Not on-prem unless you make it so.
- Prove it in an artefact: Model catalogue lags the lab.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Managed platforms and inference hosts are the middle path: models in your cloud account or a host, without you owning GPUs. I pick them when identity, region and contract matter and I still do not want CUDA on-call) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry: in-account, IAM, region.
Inference hosts: open weights, their GPUs.
Still a vendor; still wrap.
Not on-prem unless you make it so.
Model catalogue lags the lab.

questions.q: What is the third path between a public API and self-host?
questions.a: Managed cloud platforms in your account, and inference hosts that serve open weights for you.

questions.q: A bank has an AWS account and a no-public-API rule. Where do you start?
questions.a: Bedrock (or equivalent) in-region with IAM and a private link, after the model exists there. Wrapper stays yours.

questions.q: A slide says 'on-prem' but they call Bedrock. Correct the language.
questions.a: The model runs in the cloud account. That may meet the questionnaire. It is not a box in their DC unless they chose that.

questions.q: When is a serverless open-weight host enough?
questions.a: When the licence allows it, the data class allows another processor, and you do not want GPUs. Pin the slug and eval.

questions.q: What do you still wrap?
questions.a: The invoke call. Evals and prompts stay portable when the path changes.

## What it is

Other axes besides path: **small vs large**, **dense vs MoE**, **general vs specialised** (code, embed, rerank, vision), **reasoning vs not**, **text-only vs multimodal**. A shortlist that only says "GPT vs Llama" is incomplete. A 8B embedder is not a chatbot. A reasoning model is not a classifier.

Write the axes you care about for *this* workload. Do not enumerate the industry.

Multimodal means the input (or output) is not only text. It has a different price and failure mode (it can misread a screenshot).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want you to add two or three of these without being asked. On the job this is how you avoid using a giant chat model as an embedder.

They will ask for an example of specialised (embedding, code, rerank).

## How it works + one small example

Ticket product:

- Classify: small instruct, not reasoning
- Embed for search: embedding model
- Answer: general or reasoning if hard, plus RAG
- Screenshot of a bill: multimodal or an OCR tool

Do not send screenshots to a text-only model and hope.

When you compare two "70B"s, say dense vs MoE and reasoning vs not. Those change the bill.

## Failure modes

1. **One model for every axis.**

2. **Chat model as embedder.**

3. **Text-only on screenshots.**

4. **Ignoring reasoning as a class.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I also distinguish small/large, dense/MoE, general/specialised, reasoning, and modality. A shortlist that only names brands is incomplete. I pick the axis that the workload actually uses.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. - Prove it in an artefact: Size, density, speciality, reasoning, modality.
- Prove it in an artefact: Embedders, rerankers, code models are different tools.
- Prove it in an artefact: Reasoning is a class, not a brand.
- Prove it in an artefact: Multimodal has its own errors and prices.
- Prove it in an artefact: One chat model for everything is lazy.
- Prove it in an artefact: Name the axes on the shortlist.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

questions.a: Small vs large, dense vs MoE, general vs specialised, reasoning vs not, text vs multimodal.

questions.a: An embedding model, not a chat completion. Different training and interface.

questions.q: A team sends receipt photos to a text-only model. What should they use?
questions.a: A multimodal model or an OCR tool, then a text model on the extracted fields.

there-is-no-universally-best-llm.explain:
## What it is

There is **no universally best LLM**. The best model is the one that **wins your workload** on **quality, latency, cost, context, modality, privacy, and features** — the eight dimensions of M1.12. A winner on a public chat arena can lose your JSON extract. A winner on your extract can lose a planning task.

Internalise this or you will chase leaderboards and vendor keynotes forever.

The sentence is a principle, not a shrug. You still pick, with an eval.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers listen for this sentence. On the job it is how you end a religious argument. They will ask "so how do you pick" — point at the workflow in M1.12.

They will punish "I always use X".

## How it works + one small example

When someone asks for the best model, ask "for which task". Then: shortlist 2–3, run the golden set, pick.

Keep two winners if the tasks disagree (cheap classify, expensive plan). A fleet is normal.

Write the principle at the top of the model-choice doc so the next keynote does not overturn it without a measurement.

## Failure modes

1. **A company-wide favourite** with no eval.

2. **Arena rank as destiny.**

3. **One model for every task.**

4. **Shrug** — you still must pick.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

There is no universally best LLM. The best is the one that wins this workload on our dimensions. I shortlist, I measure, I will run a fleet if tasks disagree. I will not pick from a keynote.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: No global winner.
- Prove it in an artefact: Best = wins this workload.
- Prove it in an artefact: Arena rank does not transfer.
- Prove it in an artefact: Fleets are normal.
- Prove it in an artefact: Still pick, with an eval.
- Prove it in an artefact: Write the principle down.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: There is no universally best LLM. The best is the one that wins this workload on our dimensions. I shortlist, I measure, I will run a fleet if tasks disagree. I will not pick from a keynote. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

## One more pass

Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. Add the second write-up to your notes and keep the first as the interview line. That second pass is usually what fills the gap between recognising the topic and being able to debug it under time pressure.
keyPoints: No global winner.
Best = wins this workload.
Arena rank does not transfer.
Fleets are normal.
Still pick, with an eval.
Write the principle down.

questions.q: Is there a universally best LLM?
questions.a: No. The best model depends on the workload and the constraints.

questions.q: Someone asks you to standardise on last week's arena winner. What do you do?
questions.a: Run our golden set. If it loses JSON extract, keep the extract model. Maybe use the winner on chat only.

questions.q: A company has one approved model for classify, plan, and embed. Symptom?
questions.a: Two of those tasks are probably overpaying or underperforming. Split the fleet.

questions.q: How do you end a brand argument in a meeting?
questions.a: Write the task and the dimensions on the board. Schedule the eval. No winner until the table is filled.

questions.q: Does 'no best' mean 'no decision'?
questions.a: No. It means the decision is local and measured.

knowledge-cutoffs.explain:
## What it is

A model's **knowledge stops at its training cutoff** (plus whatever post-train mix they added). **Anything newer** must arrive through **context, retrieval, or tools**. The cutoff is a date on the card, often fuzzy. It is not "the model knows 2024" as a personality.

A cutoff is why the model invents last week's CEO or a sports score. It is also why you do not use it as a news product without a tool.

Some products browse. That is a tool, not a later cutoff of the weights.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask why the model missed a 2025 API. On the job this is the freshness design. They want: cutoff + retrieve/tools, not a bigger model.

They will ask where you find the cutoff (card, vendor doc — and still verify).

## How it works + one small example

Read the card. Treat the date as "do not trust world facts after this without a source".

Product: news, prices, docs, release notes → retrieve or browse. Evergreen style and language → weights may suffice.

When the vendor updates the cutoff, re-eval; behaviour changes too.

Do not put "knowledge cutoff: 2023" in the system prompt as your only freshness strategy. The model will still guess.

## Failure modes

1. **Guessing after the cutoff.**

2. **A bigger model as freshness.**

3. **Prompt-only cutoff warnings.**

4. **Confusing browse with weights.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Weights have a cutoff. Newer facts come from context, retrieval or tools. I do not ask a bigger model for last night's news, and I do not treat browse as a later cutoff of the file.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Cutoff = end of the training mix.
- Prove it in an artefact: Newer facts need context, RAG, or tools.
- Prove it in an artefact: Browse is a tool.
- Prove it in an artefact: Bigger ≠ fresher.
- Prove it in an artefact: Re-eval when the cutoff moves.
- Prove it in an artefact: A prompt warning is not a strategy.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Weights have a cutoff. Newer facts come from context, retrieval or tools. I do not ask a bigger model for last night's news, and I do not treat browse as a later cutoff of the file) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).
keyPoints: Cutoff = end of the training mix.
Newer facts need context, RAG, or tools.
Browse is a tool.
Bigger ≠ fresher.
Re-eval when the cutoff moves.
A prompt warning is not a strategy.

questions.q: What is a knowledge cutoff?
questions.a: The date after which the frozen weights were not trained on the world. Newer facts must be supplied at inference.

questions.q: How do you answer 'who won last night'?
questions.a: A search or stats tool, then the model writes the sentence. Not the weights.

questions.q: A PM wants a bigger model so it 'knows 2026'. What do you say?
questions.a: Scale is not a time machine. Retrieve or browse.

questions.q: Where do you look up the cutoff?
questions.a: The model card or vendor doc, then treat it as approximate. Still ground anything that must be right.

questions.q: Does a browse-enabled product have a later cutoff in the weights?
questions.a: No. It has a tool. The file is still frozen.

versions-snapshots-deprecations.explain:
## What it is

Model **names** move. **`gpt-x`** today may be a **different snapshot** tomorrow. Vendors **deprecate** ids. **Pin a dated snapshot** in production (`gpt-x-2025-01-15` or the platform's version). **Re-test** when you move. Aliases are for demos and for a controlled upgrade path, not for an unattended hot path.

Deprecation is a calendar event. Own it like you own a library bump.

This is the same idea as image tags versus latest.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a silent alias move is a quality incident. Interviewers want pin + re-eval. They will ask what you do when a deprecation mail arrives (schedule the eval, do not ignore).

They will punish "we just use the latest".

## How it works + one small example

Config: `model: gpt-x-2025-01-15` in prod. `model: gpt-x` in a nightly shadow that compares the golden set. Promote when the delta is acceptable.

When the mail says 90 days to deprecation: ticket, eval, migrate, do not discover it on the error dashboard.

Log the resolved snapshot if the API returns it. Store it with the request id so a bug is replayable.

## Failure modes

1. **Alias in prod.**

2. **Ignoring deprecation mail.**

3. **No golden set** so you cannot re-test.

4. **No logged snapshot.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pin a dated snapshot in production. Aliases move. When a version changes I re-run the golden set. Deprecation is a scheduled migration, not a surprise 400.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Aliases move; snapshots pin.
- Prove it in an artefact: Deprecation is a calendar event.
- Prove it in an artefact: Re-eval on every move.
- Prove it in an artefact: Shadow the new alias.
- Prove it in an artefact: Log the resolved id.
- Prove it in an artefact: Same lesson as Docker latest.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (I pin a dated snapshot in production. Aliases move. When a version changes I re-run the golden set. Deprecation is a scheduled migration, not a surprise 400) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

Re-eval on every move.

Log the resolved id.

questions.q: Why pin a snapshot?
questions.a: The friendly name can point at a new function. A dated id stays put until you move.

questions.q: A deprecation email lands. What is the process?
questions.a: Ticket, run the golden set on the replacement, compare, migrate, then drop the old id before the deadline.

questions.q: Quality dropped on Tuesday and nobody shipped. Cause?
questions.a: An alias moved. Pin, log the snapshot, shadow next time.

questions.q: Where do you use the alias?
questions.a: In a controlled shadow or a staging experiment, not on the unattended hot path.

questions.q: What do you log besides the alias?
questions.a: The resolved snapshot if the API provides it, plus your config value.

open-weight-licensing.explain:
## What it is

**Read the licence** before you build on an open-weight model. **Permissive** (Apache, MIT-like) is not the same as **restricted-use** (no commercial, no certain industries, share-alike, acceptable-use). **Llama-style** community licences often allow commercial use with **conditions** (user caps, attribution). **Non-commercial** weights cannot go in a paid product.

"Open" on a card is not permission. Legal should see the file, not a tweet.

Outputs may have their own terms (no training on the output). That is a later item too.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a launch dies when legal finds a non-commercial clause. Interviewers want you to say "I read the licence" and name two kinds. They will ask who signs it (legal, not the intern who downloaded the weights).

They will punish "Hugging Face means we can use it".

## How it works + one small example

Before the prototype becomes a product: copy the licence text into the ticket, highlight commercial, territorial, user-count, and attribution clauses. Legal signs.

If you cannot accept the clause, pick another checkpoint or an API whose terms you already have.

Do not fine-tune a non-commercial base into a commercial child and hope. The base licence usually still applies.

Attribution: if required, put it in the docs, not only in a comment.

## Failure modes

1. **Shipping without a read.**

2. **Hugging Face as a licence.**

3. **Ignoring user-count clauses.**

4. **Fine-tune to launder a licence.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read the open-weight licence before we build. Permissive, restricted, and non-commercial are different. Hugging Face is a host, not a permission slip. Legal signs, not the download button.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Open weight ≠ permission.
- Prove it in an artefact: Permissive vs restricted vs non-commercial.
- Prove it in an artefact: Some community licences have user caps.
- Prove it in an artefact: Legal reads the file.
- Prove it in an artefact: Fine-tunes inherit the base terms unless told otherwise.
- Prove it in an artefact: HF is a host.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (I read the open-weight licence before we build. Permissive, restricted, and non-commercial are different. Hugging Face is a host, not a permission slip. Legal signs, not the download button) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

Permissive vs restricted vs non-commercial.
Some community licences have user caps.

questions.q: Why check an open-weight licence?
questions.a: Terms differ: commercial use, industry bans, user caps, attribution. Open is not a single permission.

questions.q: Who signs off?
questions.a: Legal, with the licence text in the ticket. Not the engineer who ran git lfs.

questions.q: You fine-tuned a non-commercial checkpoint for a paid app. Problem?
questions.a: The base terms usually still bind the child. Pick a different base or a licensed API.

questions.a: Commercial use, territory, user-count, attribution, acceptable use, and any output-training bans.

questions.a: No. The repo's licence file does. Some repos are research-only.

deprecation-and-snapshot-pins.explain:
## What it is

**Pin a dated snapshot in production; aliases move under you.** This is the operational restatement of versions and deprecations. The pin lives in **config**, the **shadow** lives in **CI or a cron**, and the **calendar** lives in a **ticket** when the vendor announces a kill date.

If you cannot name the snapshot running in prod right now, you are on an alias.

Two items in this module sound alike on purpose: one is the landscape fact, this is the habit.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers may ask twice to see if you operationalise it. On the job this is a checklist item next to `uv.lock` and image digests.

They want the config line, not the philosophy.

## How it works + one small example

`MODEL_ID=claude-...-2025xxxx` in the platform secret. A weekly job calls the alias, runs n golden items, posts a diff. Humans promote.

On-call runbook: if quality cliffs, check whether the pin is what you think (`curl` the config, log line). Do not "restart to pick up latest".

When you must move, change the pin in one PR with the eval attached.

## Failure modes

1. **Pin in a notebook** not in prod config.

2. **No shadow.**

3. **Restart to get latest** as a fix.

4. **Unknown snapshot** on the incident call.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prod config holds a dated snapshot. A shadow watches the alias. I can name the id on the incident call. I do not restart to pick up latest.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Pin in prod config, not a notebook.
- Prove it in an artefact: Shadow the alias.
- Prove it in an artefact: Name the id on the incident call.
- Prove it in an artefact: Move via a PR with eval.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not restart for 'latest'.
- Prove it in an artefact: Same habit as lockfiles and image digests.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Prod config holds a dated snapshot. A shadow watches the alias. I can name the id on the incident call. I do not restart to pick up latest. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

## One more pass

Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. Add the second write-up to your notes and keep the first as the interview line. That second pass is usually what fills the gap between recognising the topic and being able to debug it under time pressure.

questions.q: Where does the pin live?
questions.a: In production config / secrets, logged on every request. Not only in a slide.

questions.q: What watches the moving alias?
questions.a: A shadow job on the golden set that posts a diff. Humans promote.

questions.a: They were on an alias or a floating tag. Restarts can move you. Pins should not change on restart.

questions.a: The golden-set delta and a rollback note (the previous id).

license-vs-weights-vs-api-terms.explain:
## What it is

Three documents. The **weight licence** (if you download). The **API terms** (if you call). The **output / usage policy** (what you may do with completions, including **no training on outputs** and acceptable use). **Open weights can still forbid commercial use or training on outputs.** An API can forbid sending their outputs into another model. These are **independent**.

You can be fine on the weights and dead on the API terms, or the reverse.

Read the one that matches the path you actually take — and the output clause either way.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask whether open weights mean you can train a student model on the teacher's outputs (often no). On the job this is the distillation / synthetic-data conversation. They want three documents, not one vibe.

They will punish "the weights are Apache so we can do anything with the API too".

## How it works + one small example

Path API: DPA + API terms + usage policy. Path open: weight licence + host terms if any + output clause. Path platform: the cloud agreement + the model provider's pass-through terms.

Synthetic data: if the teacher forbids training on outputs, do not distill. Pick a teacher whose terms allow it, or use your own gold.

Keep a one-page "what we may do" in the repo for engineers who will otherwise paste completions into a train set.

## Failure modes

1. **One document for three questions.**

2. **Distilling against the terms.**

3. **Apache weights + ignored host terms.**

4. **No written 'what we may do'.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Licence, weights, and API terms are different papers. Open weights can still ban commercial use or training on outputs. I read the paper that matches our path, and I do not distill against the output clause.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Three docs: weight licence, API terms, output policy.
- Prove it in an artefact: They do not inherit automatically.
- Prove it in an artefact: Open weights can still restrict commercial use and distillation.
- Prove it in an artefact: API outputs often cannot train other models.
- Prove it in an artefact: Write what we may do.
- Prove it in an artefact: Path decides which paper is binding.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Licence, weights, and API terms are different papers. Open weights can still ban commercial use or training on outputs. I read the paper that matches our path, and I do not distill against the output clause) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

They do not inherit automatically.
Open weights can still restrict commercial use and distillation.
API outputs often cannot train other models.
Write what we may do.
Path decides which paper is binding.

questions.q: Why are licence, weights and API terms different?
questions.a: One governs the checkpoint file, one the HTTP service, one what you may do with outputs. They can disagree.

questions.q: You want to distill a student from a closed API. First step?
questions.a: Read the output / usage terms. If they ban training on outputs, stop or pick another teacher.

questions.q: Weights are Apache; the host TOS bans your industry. Can you ship?
questions.a: Not on that host. Run elsewhere or pick another host. Apache does not override the host contract.

questions.q: What do you put in the engineer one-pager?
questions.a: Whether we may train on outputs, commercial limits, and which path we are on. Link the real terms.

questions.q: Does an open-weight Apache file let you ignore the API you also call?
questions.a: No. The API terms still bind that path.

what-a-benchmark-is.explain:
## What it is

A **benchmark** is a **fixed set of tasks** with a **fixed scoring method**, used so different models face the **same yardstick**. MMLU, a coding suite, a math set — each is a dataset plus a metric. The yardstick is only as good as the items, the scorer, and whether the model has **seen the items**.

A benchmark is not your product. It is a **shared exam**. Shared exams leak. Shared exams saturate. Shared exams average away your edge case.

You use them to **shortlist**, then you run **your** exam.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want the definition and the humility. On the job this is how you read a card without kneeling. They will ask what a "fixed scoring method" might be (exact match, majority vote, a judge model).

They will ask why two cards with 80% MMLU can behave differently on your tickets (different tests).

## How it works + one small example

When you see a number: name the set, the metric, the shot setting (0-shot vs 5-shot), and whether it is a max over prompts. Then discount.

Build your own tiny benchmark: 50 items, a scorer, a version. That is a benchmark too — it just is not public.

Do not average a code score and a chat-preference score into "80% smart".

## Failure modes

1. **Treating the number as the product.**

2. **Mixing metrics.**

3. **Ignoring shots and prompts.**

4. **No private set.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A benchmark is a fixed exam with a fixed scorer. I use it to shortlist. I do not ship on it. My 50 labelled tickets are the exam that matters.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Fixed tasks + fixed scorer = benchmark.
- Prove it in an artefact: A shared exam, not your product.
- Prove it in an artefact: Note shots, prompts, leaks.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not average unlike metrics.
- Prove it in an artefact: Your set is a benchmark too.
- Prove it in an artefact: Shortlist, then local eval.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: A benchmark is a fixed exam with a fixed scorer. I use it to shortlist. I do not ship on it. My 50 labelled tickets are the exam that matters. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: Fixed tasks + fixed scorer = benchmark.
A shared exam, not your product.
Note shots, prompts, leaks.
Do not average unlike metrics.
Your set is a benchmark too.
Shortlist, then local eval.

questions.q: What is a benchmark?
questions.a: A fixed task set with a fixed scoring method so models can be compared on the same yardstick.

questions.q: What do you read next to an 80%?
questions.a: Which set, which metric, 0-shot vs few-shot, and whether it is a best-of prompt. Then discount.

questions.q: Two models have the same MMLU and one fails your JSON. Why is that allowed?
questions.a: Different exams. MMLU is not JSON extract on your schema.

questions.q: How do you make a private benchmark?
questions.a: Versioned items, a written scorer, a held-out split. Run every snapshot.

questions.q: Why do shared exams leak?
questions.a: They sit on the internet. Training mixes and contamination can include them.

benchmarks-quoted-on-model-cards.explain:
## What it is

Cards quote **knowledge/reasoning** tests (**MMLU**, **GPQA**), **coding** tests, **math** tests, sometimes **multimodal**. Roughly: MMLU is broad multiple-choice knowledge; GPQA is harder expert-ish questions; HumanEval-style is code unit tests; MATH/GSM8K-style is written math. You need the **gist**, not the paper.

These numbers are **advertising-adjacent**. They are useful to **drop a model that scores 20% on code** if you need code. They are useless to **pick a winner** for your tickets.

Always check **whether the card reports 0-shot or 5-shot** and **which checkpoint** (base vs instruct).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will say "MMLU" and expect a one-liner. On the job you skim the table in 60 seconds. They will ask which bench matters for a SQL bot (code + execution, not MMLU).

They will punish memorising paper titles without the gist.

## How it works + one small example

60-second card read:

- Need code? Look at code benches, then still run your tests.
- Need hard reasoning? GPQA-ish, then still run your items.
- Need chat taste? Those MC suites are the wrong type — look at a preference arena as a hint, then your own raters.

If the card omits the bench that matches your task, that is information. They may be hiding a weak score.

Do not rank three models by MMLU to 0.1 points. That is noise.

## Failure modes

1. **Picking by 0.1 MMLU.**

2. **Using MMLU for a SQL bot.**

3. **Ignoring base vs instruct** on the table.

4. **Memorising without gist.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I know what MMLU, GPQA, code and math suites roughly measure. I use them to drop obvious mismatches, not to pick a winner for our task. 0.1 points is noise.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: MMLU ≈ broad MC knowledge; GPQA ≈ harder questions.
- Prove it in an artefact: Code suites ≈ unit-test pass; math suites ≈ written problems.
- Prove it in an artefact: Use them to drop, not to crown.
- Prove it in an artefact: Check shots and checkpoint.
- Prove it in an artefact: 0.1 points is noise.
- Prove it in an artefact: Missing a relevant bench is a signal.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: I know what MMLU, GPQA, code and math suites roughly measure. I use them to drop obvious mismatches, not to pick a winner for our task. 0.1 points is noise. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: MMLU ≈ broad MC knowledge; GPQA ≈ harder questions.
Code suites ≈ unit-test pass; math suites ≈ written problems.
Use them to drop, not to crown.
Check shots and checkpoint.
0.1 points is noise.
Missing a relevant bench is a signal.

questions.q: What does MMLU roughly measure?
questions.a: Broad multiple-choice knowledge and some reasoning across many subjects. Not your ticket schema.

questions.q: Which published benches would you glance at for a code assistant?
questions.a: HumanEval-style or a coding leaderboard, then you still run your repo's tests.

questions.q: A card leads with MMLU and omits code scores for a 'coding model'. What do you think?
questions.a: They may be hiding a weak code number. Run code evals yourself.

questions.q: Two models are 71.2 and 71.4 MMLU. How do you pick?
questions.a: You do not pick on that. You run your set. That gap is noise.

questions.q: Why does 5-shot vs 0-shot matter on a card?
questions.a: Few-shot can lift the number. Compare like with like.

kinds-of-leaderboard.explain:
## What it is

Three useful kinds. **Human-preference** arenas (**LMArena / Chatbot Arena**): people vote on blind pairs — good for **chat taste**, bad as a **task SLA**. **Aggregated dashboards**: mix capability, cost, latency — useful **maps**, still not your task. **Open-model leaderboards**: academic-style suites on downloadable models — good to **scan the open field**.

Each has a **different definition of good**. Mixing them into one number is how you get a meaningless rank.

Read the kind before the rank.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will mention Arena. They want "preference, not exact-match" and "does not transfer". On the job this is how you refuse a screenshot of rank #3 as a decision.

They will ask for a second kind (open LLM leaderboard, or a cost/latency dashboard).

## How it works + one small example

Use Arena: "is this model not terrible at general chat?" Use open leaderboard: "which 8B instruct is in the conversation for self-host?" Use a cost dashboard: "what is the cheap-fast cluster?" Then leave the boards and run your items.

If a stakeholder sends an Arena plot, thank them and book the eval slot.

Do not average Arena Elo with MMLU. Different units.

## Failure modes

1. **Arena as SLA.**

2. **Averaging unlike boards.**

3. **Ignoring who the voters are.**

4. **Open board for a closed-only decision** or the reverse.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Preference arenas, aggregated cost/quality dashboards, and open-model suites are different kinds of board. I read the kind, I use them as maps, and I do not ship a rank.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Arena = human preference on chat pairs.
- Prove it in an artefact: Dashboards mix capability, cost, latency.
- Prove it in an artefact: Open boards scan downloadable models.
- Prove it in an artefact: Different definitions of good.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not average unlike ranks.
- Prove it in an artefact: Maps, not SLAs.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Preference arenas, aggregated cost/quality dashboards, and open-model suites are different kinds of board. I read the kind, I use them as maps, and I do not ship a rank.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.
keyPoints: Arena = human preference on chat pairs.
Dashboards mix capability, cost, latency.
Open boards scan downloadable models.
Different definitions of good.
Do not average unlike ranks.
Maps, not SLAs.

questions.q: Name three kinds of leaderboard.
questions.a: Human-preference arenas, aggregated capability/cost/latency dashboards, and open-model academic-style boards.

questions.q: What is Arena good and bad for?
questions.a: Good as a chat-taste hint. Bad as a reliability number for your extractor.

questions.q: A VP wants the Arena #1 as the only production model. Your move?
questions.a: Run the golden set. Keep a cheaper specialist if it wins the task. Explain that Elo is preference, not our metric.

questions.q: When do you open the open-LLM board?
questions.a: When you are shortlisting downloadable instruct models to self-host or host.

questions.q: Why not average Elo and MMLU?
questions.a: Different scales, different definitions of good, different contamination stories.

why-rank-does-not-transfer.explain:
## What it is

A leaderboard rank **rarely transfers** because **your prompts**, **your tasks**, **your raters' definition of good**, and **averaged scores** are different. A model that wins casual chat can fail a terse JSON schema. A model that wins coding contests can fail your proprietary DSL. Averages hide the slice you care about.

Transfer is an empirical claim. The default is **it does not transfer**. The experiment is **your set**.

This is "no universally best" applied to boards.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want this sentence. On the job it is the comment on every Slack screenshot. They will ask for a concrete mismatch (JSON vs chat).

They will punish "it is #2 so it will be #2 for us".

## How it works + one small example

Keep a one-slide picture: Arena top-3 vs your extract exact-match. The order will shuffle. That slide pays for itself in every planning cycle.

When a rank *does* match your set, say so. You still re-check on the next snapshot.

If you only have 15 items, say the transfer claim is weak. Grow the set.

## Failure modes

1. **Copying the rank into the ADR.**

2. **No slice** — only a global average.

3. **15 items** as proof of transfer.

4. **Never updating** after a snapshot.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Ranks do not transfer by default. Different prompts, tasks and definitions of good. I show the shuffle on our slice and I still re-check the next snapshot.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Different prompts, tasks, raters.
- Prove it in an artefact: Averages hide your slice.
- Prove it in an artefact: Default: no transfer.
- Prove it in an artefact: Prove transfer with your set.
- Prove it in an artefact: Orders shuffle across metrics.
- Prove it in an artefact: Re-check snapshots.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Ranks do not transfer by default. Different prompts, tasks and definitions of good. I show the shuffle on our slice and I still re-check the next snapshot) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

Orders shuffle across metrics.

questions.q: Why does a leaderboard rank rarely transfer?
questions.a: Your prompts, task, and definition of good differ, and public scores are averages that hide your slice.

questions.q: Give a mismatch example.
questions.a: An Arena-winning chat model fails a strict JSON schema; a mid-rank model passes because it was post-trained for instructions.

questions.q: An ADR says 'we picked #2'. What is missing?
questions.a: The local metric, the set, and the date. #2 of what, when.

questions.q: How do you show non-transfer in a meeting?
questions.a: A table: public rank vs our exact-match. The order shuffles. That is the slide.

questions.q: When might a rank weakly transfer?
questions.a: When your task is close to the board's (general chat vs Arena). Still measure.

what-inflates-published-scores.explain:
## What it is

Scores inflate via **contamination** (items in the train mix), **saturation** (everyone is 90%+ so the bench is dull), **overfitting to public tests** (prompting and training against the known set), and **favourable run configs** (best-of-n, generous judges, cherry-picked shots). A high number can be **real capability** or **exam technique**.

You cannot see which from the card alone. You can **discount** and **run your own set**.

This pairs with the contamination item later.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want two inflation causes. On the job this is how you stay calm when a card jumps 8 points. They will ask what you would trust more (a private set, a live A/B).

They will punish taking a best-of-32 number as a single-sample SLA.

## How it works + one small example

Discount checklist: is the bench old and public? Is everyone saturated? Did they report best-of? Did they use a judge that likes verbosity? Then cut the number in your head and move on.

If you must compare cards, compare the same bench, same shots, same date. Still do not ship on it.

Your set should stay private and rotate items so you do not contaminate yourself.

## Failure modes

1. **Best-of-n as the SLA.**

2. **A saturated bench** as a ranking.

3. **No discount.**

4. **Publishing your only eval set.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Published scores inflate from contamination, saturation, overfitting and friendly configs. I discount the card and I keep a private, rotating set. Best-of-n is not my p50.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Contamination, saturation, overfit, friendly configs.
- Prove it in an artefact: Best-of is not a single-call SLA.
- Prove it in an artefact: Saturated benches do not rank.
- Prove it in an artefact: Discount, then local eval.
- Prove it in an artefact: Keep your set private and rotating.
- Prove it in an artefact: An 8-point card jump is a reason to be curious, not to cut over.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Published scores inflate from contamination, saturation, overfitting and friendly configs. I discount the card and I keep a private, rotating set. Best-of-n is not my p50. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: Contamination, saturation, overfit, friendly configs.
Best-of is not a single-call SLA.
Saturated benches do not rank.
Discount, then local eval.
Keep your set private and rotating.
An 8-point card jump is a reason to be curious, not to cut over.

questions.q: Name three things that inflate published scores.
questions.a: Train-set contamination, saturated benches, overfitting to the public test, best-of-n or friendly judges.

questions.q: A card reports best-of-32. How do you read it?
questions.a: As an upper bound, not as what one production call will do. Ask for pass@1 or run it yourself at n=1.

questions.q: Everyone is at 92% on a 2020 suite. Can you rank on it?
questions.a: Not usefully. The bench is saturated. Pick a harder or private set.

questions.q: How do you avoid contaminating yourself?
questions.a: Keep the golden set private, rotate items, do not paste it into blog posts or prompts that might be logged into someone else's train mix.

questions.q: Is a jump of 8 points on a public bench always real?
questions.a: Not always. New contamination, a new prompt, or a new judge can move the number.

from-leaderboard-to-shortlist.explain:
## What it is

Boards are good at **one thing**: **narrowing a crowded field to a shortlist**. Then you **judge the shortlist on your own examples**. Three models, not thirty. The board saved you the weekend of trying every 7B on Hugging Face. It did not pick the winner.

Write the shortlist rule: "top 5 on the open board in our size/licence band" or "the three vendors we already have a DPA with". Then stop reading ranks.

This is the constructive use of everything above.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want the workflow, not only the skepticism. On the job this is how you use Arena without worshipping it. They will ask how many you shortlist (2–4).

They will punish "I ignore all boards" (waste) and "I only use boards" (malpractice).

## How it works + one small example

Example: need an 8B commercial-ok instruct. Filter licence and size, take the top handful on an open board plus one vendor 8B-class API, run your 50 items, pick.

Time-box the board hour. The rest of the week is the local eval and the cost table.

When the board changes next month, you do not automatically change the shortlist. You glance, then decide whether to add a candidate.

## Failure modes

1. **Thirty-model bake-off.**

2. **Shortlist = winner.**

3. **Re-shortlisting every tweet.**

4. **Ignoring licence in the filter.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Leaderboards narrow a crowded field to a shortlist. I pick 2–4 with a written filter, then I run our examples. The board does not get a vote in the final table.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Boards: shortlist, not winner.
- Prove it in an artefact: 2–4 candidates.
- Prove it in an artefact: Filter size, licence, path first.
- Prove it in an artefact: Time-box the board hour.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not re-shortlist every tweet.
- Prove it in an artefact: Local eval is the vote.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. contamination-and-train-test-overlap.explain:
## What it is

A **high score can mean the item leaked into training**. Public items, GitHub copies of HumanEval, and blog reproductions sit in crawls. **Contamination** is train–test overlap. You cannot fully audit a closed model. You can **assume it** on famous items and **prefer private, recent, or dynamically generated tests**.

Your own set can contaminate if you paste it into a vendor UI that trains on inputs — read the terms.

This is why "it nailed MMLU" is a weak brag in 2026.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will say contamination and expect a definition plus a mitigation. On the job this is why you do not hire a model on HumanEval screenshots.

They will ask how you would test a code model fairly (hidden tests, new problems).

## How it works + one small example

Mitigations: private items, rotate, generate variants, execute code against hidden tests, use last week's tickets not a 2020 suite.

If you must use a public bench, treat a high score as an upper bound.

For vendors: prefer terms that say they do not train on API data, and still do not paste your only gold set.

When a model fails your private set and aces the public one, believe yours.

## Failure modes

1. **Hiring on HumanEval screenshots.**

2. **Pasting the gold set** into a train-on-input UI.

3. **Never rotating** items.

4. **Trusting a closed model's 'we did not contaminate'** as proof.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A high public score can be leakage. I assume contamination on famous items, I keep a private rotating set, and I believe that set when it disagrees with the card.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Contamination = train–test overlap.
- Prove it in an artefact: Famous items leak.
- Prove it in an artefact: Private, recent, hidden tests.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not paste gold into train-on-input UIs.
- Prove it in an artefact: Public high score is an upper bound.
- Prove it in an artefact: Believe your set when it disagrees.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

I assume contamination on famous items, I keep a private rotating set, and I believe that set when it disagrees with the card.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

your-task-is-the-only-leaderboard-that-s.explain:
## What it is

**Public ranks shortlist; your eval decides.** The only leaderboard that ships is **the one you run on your task**, with **your metric**, **your snapshot**, **your prompt**. Everything else is homework.

Write that sentence in the model-choice doc. When a keynote lands, you already know what you will do: add a candidate if you want, run the set, or ignore.

This is the module's last word and M1.12's first.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want the slogan. On the job it is how a staff engineer ends the meeting. They will ask what "your eval" contains (items, metric, pin, date).

Hang the latest table in the repo or the wiki. The next argument starts from the table, not from Twitter.

1. **Shipping on a keynote.**

2. **Empty set.**

3. **A set nobody owns.**

4. **Table not dated.**
