eight-dimensions-for-model-choice.explain:
## What it is

Evaluate models on **eight dimensions**: **capability**, **quality**, **latency**, **cost**, **context**, **modalities**, **privacy & deployment**, **product features**. A pick that only uses one (usually quality or a brand) is incomplete. The dimensions are the rest of this module, one card each, plus how you read cards and the workflow.

Write them on the whiteboard before you name a vendor. The shortlist must have at least a note on each, even if the note is "n/a".

This is the checklist. The later cards are the flesh.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how you choose a model. If you start with a brand you have already lost. On the job this list is the decision-doc template. They want you to rattle six of the eight without a slide.

They will ask which dimension kills a candidate first (often privacy or latency).

## How it works + one small example

Template row: model id, can-it (capability), how-reliably (quality + set), p95, $/task, window, text/vision, path (API/platform/self), tools/JSON/stream/cache.

Fill three rows. Cross out anyone who fails a hard constraint (must be in-region, must be <800 ms, must have structured output). Rank the rest on quality/cost.

Hang the eight words in the README of the eval repo.

## Failure modes

1. **Quality-only.**

2. **Brand-first.**

3. **Skipping a hard constraint** until after the bake-off.

4. **Eight slides of prose** and no table.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I choose on eight dimensions: capability, quality, latency, cost, context, modality, privacy/deployment, features. I write them before I name a vendor, I fail hard constraints first, and I fill a table for the rest.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Eight dimensions, not a brand.
- Prove it in an artefact: Fail hard constraints first.
- Prove it in an artefact: Table beats prose.
- Prove it in an artefact: Quality is one column.
- Prove it in an artefact: n/a is an allowed cell.
- Prove it in an artefact: This list is the module.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (I choose on eight dimensions: capability, quality, latency, cost, context, modality, privacy/deployment, features. I write them before I name a vendor, I fail hard constraints first, and I fill a table for the rest) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

Fail hard constraints first.

Quality is one column.
n/a is an allowed cell.
This list is the module.

questions.q: Name the eight dimensions for model choice.
questions.a: Capability, quality, latency, cost, context, modalities, privacy and deployment, product features.

questions.q: What do you write first on the whiteboard?
questions.a: The eight words and the hard constraints. Then vendor names.

questions.q: A bake-off ignored region and picked a public API. What happened?
questions.a: They skipped privacy/deployment until too late. Fail that column first next time.

questions.q: How do you use the table?
questions.a: Cross out hard-constraint fails. Rank the rest on quality per dollar and p95.

questions.q: Why is capability different from quality?
questions.a: Capability is 'can it at all'. Quality is 'how reliably on our set'.

capability.explain:
## What it is

**Capability: can it perform the task at all?** Function calling, vision, 100k context, JSON mode, a language, a 70-page contract — some models **cannot**. This is a **yes/no (or not without a wrap)** filter, not a score. If it cannot see images, it is out of a screenshot workflow. If it cannot take tools, your agent design is a fantasy.

Capability is cheap to check: read the card, try one call. Do not spend a week scoring a model that lacks the verb.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

People skip this and discover mid-bake-off that the favourite has no tools. Interviewers want the filter. On the job it is the first column you grey out.

They will ask for an example of a capability fail (text-only vs screenshots; no structured output).

## How it works + one small example

List required verbs: tools? vision? audio? 32k? JSON schema? Then tick the card. One smoke call.

If a wrap can add the capability (you OCR first), write that as a cost on the candidate, not as "it can".

Do not confuse "a demo once produced JSON" with "has JSON mode". The first is quality/luck. The second is capability.

## Failure modes

1. **Scoring a model that lacks the verb.**

2. **Demo-once as capability.**

3. **Assuming all frontier models have tools.**

4. **Forgetting language coverage.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Capability is 'can it do the verb at all'. I fail those candidates first with a card read and a smoke call. A lucky JSON demo is not JSON mode.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Yes/no filter, not a score.
- Prove it in an artefact: Tools, vision, window, JSON, language.
- Prove it in an artefact: Smoke call + card.
- Prove it in an artefact: A wrap is a cost, not a silent yes.
- Prove it in an artefact: Demo-once ≠ capability.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do this before a week of scoring.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Capability is 'can it do the verb at all'. I fail those candidates first with a card read and a smoke call. A lucky JSON demo is not JSON mode. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

## One more pass

Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. Add the second write-up to your notes and keep the first as the interview line. That second pass is usually what fills the gap between recognising the topic and being able to debug it under time pressure.
keyPoints: Yes/no filter, not a score.
Tools, vision, window, JSON, language.
Smoke call + card.
A wrap is a cost, not a silent yes.
Demo-once ≠ capability.
Do this before a week of scoring.

questions.q: What is capability in model choice?
questions.a: Whether the model can perform the task at all — the verbs and modalities — not how reliably.

questions.q: Your app needs screenshots. A text-only model is cheap. What column fails?
questions.a: Capability (and modality). OCR wrap is a different design with its own cost.

questions.q: You spent a week scoring a model that cannot call tools for an agent. What did you skip?
questions.a: The capability filter on day one.

questions.q: How do you check JSON capability?
questions.a: The card and a schema-mode call if they have one. Not a single free-form demo.

questions.q: Is 'it wrote JSON once' capability?
questions.a: No. That is a quality anecdote. Capability is the supported feature.

quality.explain:
## What it is

**Quality: how reliably does it perform your specific task?** This is the **held-out set**, the **metric**, the **error types**. Not a card number. Not a vibe. Not "it felt smarter".

Define the metric before you run (exact match, rubric, execution). Report the number with the set version. Inspect failures — a 90% that always drops the amount field is not 90% for a finance bot.

Quality without error analysis is a vanity score.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the column people think they are filling when they quote MMLU. Interviewers want your set. On the job this is the golden set you already built in M1.11.

They will ask what you do with the 10% (human, retry, abstain).

## How it works + one small example

50–200 items, versioned. Metric written down. Two reviewers on a sample if the metric is a judge. Slice by type (empty ticket, long ticket, Hindi).

Look at 20 failures. If they are one bug, fix the prompt and re-run. If they are a long tail, decide the human path.

Do not change the metric after you see the scores. That is p-hacking a bake-off.

## Failure modes

1. **Card number as quality.**

2. **No failure inspection.**

3. **Changing the metric** after seeing scores.

4. **One slice** (only easy items).

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Quality is reliability on our set, with a written metric and an error look. A card number is not quality. I will not change the metric after I see the scores.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Your set, your metric.
- Prove it in an artefact: Inspect failures.
- Prove it in an artefact: Slice the score.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not p-hack the metric.
- Prove it in an artefact: Plan the 10%.
- Prove it in an artefact: Card ≠ quality.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Quality is reliability on our set, with a written metric and an error look. A card number is not quality. I will not change the metric after I see the scores) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

## One more pass

Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. Add the second write-up to your notes and keep the first as the interview line. That second pass is usually what fills the gap between recognising the topic and being able to debug it under time pressure.

questions.q: What is quality in this module?
questions.a: How reliably the model does our task on a held-out set with a written metric — not a public bench.

questions.q: A model is 90% exact-match but always drops amounts. Is it shippable for invoices?
questions.a: Not without a bound on amounts. The slice that matters is failing. Inspect errors.

questions.q: After seeing scores you switch from exact match to 'judge likes it'. Problem?

questions.a: Averages hide the empty-ticket or Hindi slice you will ship to.

## What it is

**Latency: how quickly does it respond?** TTFT and total, p95 not just mean. Interactive UIs need a first token soon. Batch jobs care about total and tokens/s. Reasoning models and long outputs change the number a lot.

A model that is 2 points better and 8× slower may lose a chat product and win an offline job. Write the SLO before the bake-off.

Measure on your prompt sizes, not a 20-token hello.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want p95 and TTFT vs total. On the job this is the column that kills reasoning-as-default. They will ask how you would measure (prod-like prompts, streamed).

They will punish a mean on 10 hellos.

## How it works + one small example

Script: 50 real prompts, record TTFT, total, tokens. Report p50/p95. Include a long-context item if you have one.

SLO: "TTFT p95 < 1.5s on the chat route". Cross out anyone who cannot hit it even after shrinking the prompt.

Do not compare a 50-token answer to a 500-token answer and call the latter "slow" without tokens/s.

## Failure modes

1. **Mean only.**

2. **Hello-world prompts.**

3. **Ignoring TTFT** for chat.

4. **No SLO.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Latency is TTFT and total at p95 on our prompt sizes. I write the SLO first. A smarter-but-8×-slower model loses a chat route and may win a batch job.

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. - Prove it in an artefact: Measure on real prompt sizes.
- Prove it in an artefact: SLO before the bake-off.
- Prove it in an artefact: Chat vs batch pick different numbers.
- Prove it in an artefact: Reasoning changes the tail.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not compare unlike output lengths without tokens/s.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

I write the SLO first. A smarter-but-8×-slower model loses a chat route and may win a batch job) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. questions.q: Which latency numbers do you put on the table?
questions.a: TTFT and total at p95 (and maybe p50), measured on real prompts.

questions.q: A reasoning model is +2 quality and 8× p95. Chat or batch?
questions.a: Batch or a rare 'deep think' button. Not the default chat box unless the SLO allows it.

questions.q: The bake-off used 10 'hi' prompts. Why is the latency column junk?
questions.a: Prefill was tiny. Your real prompts are long. Re-measure.

questions.a: Users feel the tail. Reasoning and queues live in the tail.

cost.explain:
## What it is

**Cost: what will each request cost at your expected usage?** Use **tokens per successful task**, including **retries, thinking, and failures**, times **$/1M in and out**, plus **idle GPUs** if you self-host. A cheap model that needs three retries is not cheap. A dear model on 0.1% of traffic can be fine.

Write monthly $ at 1× and 10× volume. That is the column.

Do not use "it is $3/1M" as the story without your token counts.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Finance will ask. Interviewers want tokens per successful task. On the job this is how you justify a fleet (cheap classify, dear plan).

They will punish a unit-price-only slide.

## How it works + one small example

Measure tokens on the golden set. Multiply by the price list. Add retry rate. Add thinking if billed. Compare $/successful extract.

Self-host: GPU-hour / throughput × tokens, plus people.

Put a 10× volume row so a "we will grow" plan does not surprise anyone.

When quality is equal, take the cheaper. When quality differs, price the human time the errors create.

## Failure modes

1. **$/1M without token counts.**

2. **Ignoring retries and thinking.**

3. **No 10× row.**

4. **Ignoring human time** on errors.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Cost is dollars per successful task at our volume, including retries and thinking. I write a 1× and 10× monthly row. Unit price without token counts is not a story.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. ## What it is

**Context: can it accommodate the required input?** The **window** must fit **your packed prompt** (rules + retrieval + history + reserve), not a toy. A 8k model cannot take your 40k pack without a redesign. A 1M model can take it and still use it badly (M1.8).

This column is **capacity + evidence you can use that much**. Fail the ones who cannot fit. Be skeptical of the ones who "fit" a dump.

If you can redesign to 4k, more models enter the shortlist — often a win.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want window vs usable. On the job this is how you avoid picking an 8k model for a "paste the PDF" brief — or how you refuse the brief.

They will ask whether you would redesign the pack instead of buying 1M (yes, usually).

## How it works + one small example

Measure the pack: p95 tokens of production-like calls. The model must fit p95 + reserve. If not, redesign or pick a larger window.

Then, if you need >32k of *used* text, run the quality column at that length. A 1M window with a 20-point drop is a fail.

Prefer shrinking the pack. It also helps latency and cost.

## Failure modes

1. **8k model, 40k pack.**

2. **1M as architecture.**

3. **No p95 pack measurement.**

4. **Ignoring reserve.**

Context is whether the window fits our real pack, and whether quality holds at that length. I measure p95 tokens, I reserve the answer, and I would rather shrink the pack than buy a million tokens of hay.

## What it is

**Modalities: do you need text, images, audio, or video?** A text-only model **cannot** take a screenshot. A speech-to-text + LLM wrap is a **different design** (latency, errors at the ASR step). Multimodal models **misread** images and cost more. Pick the modality you need; do not buy vision "in case".

If 5% of tickets are screenshots, you might route those to a vision model or OCR, not pay vision on 100%.

This is capability's sibling, aimed at input/output types.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want a routing answer, not "we use the omni model for everything". On the job this is a cost and quality slice.

They will ask how you handle a PDF (parse first vs dump pages as images).

## How it works + one small example

Inventory inputs: 90% text, 8% images, 2% audio. Default text model. Image route: vision or OCR+text. Audio: ASR+text.

Eval vision on *your* screenshots (receipts, dark mode UI). Public vision benches will not match.

PDFs: extract text when you can; images of pages are a last resort and a token bomb.

## Failure modes

1. **Omni on 100%** for a 5% image slice.

2. **Text-only on screenshots.**

3. **No ASR error budget.**

4. **PDF-as-images by default.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I inventory modalities and I route. Vision and audio are extra cost and extra errors. I will not run an omni model on 100% of text tickets because 5% have screenshots.

- Prove it in an artefact: Extract PDF text when you can.

privacy-deployment.explain:
## What it is

**Privacy & deployment: API, managed platform in your cloud, or self-host?** This is the M1.10 path choice as a hard column. If the data class forbids a public API, those candidates die no matter their quality. If you cannot staff GPUs, self-host dies. If the model is not in-region on the platform, that row dies.

Write the data class first. Then the path. Then the models that exist on that path.

Do not run a quality bake-off on a path you cannot use.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the enterprise interview. On the job it is the column that saves a quarter of wasted work. They will ask you to order the decisions (data class → path → model).

They will punish a quality winner you cannot legally call.

## How it works + one small example

One page: data class, region, retention, who may see prompts. Then allowed paths. Then shortlist only those.

If two paths are allowed, you may still bake-off a public-API model on **synthetic** data for quality, then re-run the winner's cousin on the platform.

DPA and licence sit in this column too.

## Failure modes

1. **Quality first, legal later.**

2. **Synthetic-data winner** shipped on real PII via the public API.

3. **Self-host with no owner.**

4. **Wrong region.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Data class picks the path; the path picks the shortlist. I will not bake-off a public API on data I cannot send, and I will not self-host without an owner. Privacy is a fail-first column.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Data class → path → models.
- Prove it in an artefact: Fail this column first.
- Prove it in an artefact: API / platform / self-host.
- Prove it in an artefact: Region and retention live here.
- Prove it in an artefact: DPA and licence live here.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not quality-test an illegal path on real data.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Data class picks the path; the path picks the shortlist. I will not bake-off a public API on data I cannot send, and I will not self-host without an owner. Privacy is a fail-first column. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

## One more pass

Rewrite the how-example with different nouns (orders instead of tickets, invoices instead of prompts, images instead of containers). If the two write-ups share only the mechanism and the failure, you understand it. If they share the same sentences, you copied yourself. Add the second write-up to your notes and keep the first as the interview line. That second pass is usually what fills the gap between recognising the topic and being able to debug it under time pressure.

questions.a: A named person for serving, patching and pages. No owner, no path.

## What it is

**Product features: structured outputs, function calling, tools, streaming, caching?** These are **API verbs** that change the design. No streaming → worse chat UX. No tools → no agent. No schema mode → more glue. No prompt cache → you pay full prefill on a fat policy every time.

A model that is slightly worse on quality but has schema + cache can win the product.

Required features list next to capability. Tick them. If a wrap can fake a feature (you stream tokens you buffered — you cannot), do not lie.

## What it is

Read **cards, bench tables, pricing pages, context specs, and API docs** as a **skeptic**. Cards omit. Prices have **in vs out** and sometimes **thinking**. Context is **advertised**. Benches are **shortlists**. API docs hold the **verbs** (the features column).

A 10-minute read with a checklist beats a 2-hour vibe session. Write one sentence per source.

Critical reading is a skill: what is missing is a signal.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers may hand you a card. On the job this is Monday morning. They want the checklist, not a recitation of MMLU.

1. **Benches only.**

2. **Input price only.**

3. **Skipping API docs** (no verbs).

the-selection-workflow.explain:
## What it is

The workflow: **Define the task → Identify requirements → Shortlist → Test on your examples → Measure quality → Measure latency → Measure cost → Inspect failures → Choose**. It is a **pipeline**, not a vibe. Hard requirements (path, verbs, window) sit in "identify". Boards sit in "shortlist". Your set sits in "test/measure". Failures sit before "choose" so you do not crown a 90% that always drops amounts.

Do the steps in order. Skipping "inspect failures" is how you ship a landmine.

This is the moving picture of the eight dimensions.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want this sequence almost verbatim. On the job it is the project plan. They will ask where benches go (shortlist) and where legal goes (requirements).

They will punish "we tried a few models and liked B".

## How it works + one small example

Ticket on the wall with the nine arrows. Date each. Attach artefacts: requirements page, shortlist filter, set version, three plots, failure notes, decision.

If time is short: shrink the set, do not skip inspect. Ten failures read beat fifty scores unread.

When you choose, fill the decision log (next item).

## Failure modes

1. **Liked B.**

2. **Skip inspect.**

3. **Shortlist after you already chose.**

4. **Requirements after the bake-off.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Define, require, shortlist, test, measure quality, latency, cost, inspect failures, choose. I do it in order. I will not skip the failure pile, and I will not start with a favourite.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Nine steps, in order.
- Prove it in an artefact: Requirements before shortlist.
- Prove it in an artefact: Benches in shortlist only.
- Prove it in an artefact: Inspect before choose.
- Prove it in an artefact: Artefacts on the ticket.
- Prove it in an artefact: Ten failures read beat fifty unread.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Define, require, shortlist, test, measure quality, latency, cost, inspect failures, choose. I do it in order. I will not skip the failure pile, and I will not start with a favourite) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).

questions.a: Legal in requirements. Arena in shortlist. Neither in choose.

questions.a: Requirements, a real set, measurements, failure inspect. That is a vibe, not a workflow.

questions.a: A small real set and a look at the failures. Skip extra boards if you must.

a-written-decision-log-for-model-choice.explain:
## What it is

**Record the task, constraints, shortlist, and why you picked the winner.** A **decision log** (ADR-lite) is a page: date, owner, task, hard constraints, candidates, table (eight dimensions), failure notes, winner, **how we will notice we were wrong**, and **the pin**. Without it, six months later nobody knows why the expensive model is still on the classify route.

The log is how you re-evaluate after a provider change (next item) without folklore.

Write it the day you choose, in the repo.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask what you write down. On the job this is the artefact that survives the team. They will ask what "how we will notice" means (a metric that should not drop).

They will punish "it is in Slack".

## How it works + one small example

Template:

```
# ADR-014 pick extract-v2 model
Date, owner
Task: extract {amount, date} from tickets
Hard: in-region, JSON schema, p95 < 1.2s
Shortlist: A, B, C (filter: ...)
Table: [link]
Failures: B drops Hindi amounts
Winner: A @ pin ...
Review trigger: exact-match < 90% or price +20%
```

Link the set version. When you change the pin, add a line, do not rewrite history.

## Failure modes

1. **Slack-only.**

2. **No review trigger.**

3. **No pin.**

4. **Rewriting the ADR** instead of appending.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write a decision log the day we choose: task, constraints, shortlist, table, failures, winner, pin, and a review trigger. Six months later that page is why A is still on the route — or why we moved.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Task, constraints, shortlist, table, why, pin.
- Prove it in an artefact: A review trigger.
- Prove it in an artefact: In the repo, dated.
- Prove it in an artefact: Append on change; do not rewrite.
- Prove it in an artefact: Slack is not a log.
- Prove it in an artefact: Owner named.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: I write a decision log the day we choose: task, constraints, shortlist, table, failures, winner, pin, and a review trigger. Six months later that page is why A is still on the route — or why we moved. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

questions.q: What goes in a model-choice decision log?
questions.a: Date, owner, task, hard constraints, shortlist, the eight-dimension table, failure notes, winner, pin, and a review trigger.

questions.q: What is a review trigger?
questions.a: A metric or event that forces a revisit: quality drop, price hike, deprecation, new snapshot.

questions.q: The expensive model is still on classify and nobody knows why. What was missing?
questions.a: A log. Write one now from what you can reconstruct, then re-run the table.

questions.q: Where does it live?
questions.a: In the repo next to the eval set, not only in Slack.

questions.q: Do you rewrite the ADR when you change pins?
questions.a: No. Append a dated note so the history stays.

re-evaluating-after-a-provider-change.explain:
## What it is

**Re-run the golden set when the alias or price changes.** A new snapshot is a new function. A new price is a new cost column. A deprecation is a forced move. The decision log's **review trigger** exists for this. Do not assume quality held. Do not assume the cheaper new id is a bargain until you measure tokens per task (it may be wordier).

This is the last habit of Level 1. It closes pins, benches, and choice.

If you cannot re-run, you do not own the model — the vendor does.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask what you do when the mail says "new default model". On the job this is the cron and the PR. They want: run the set, compare the table, then move or stay.

They will punish "we will see in production".

## How it works + one small example

Triggers: alias move, price page change, deprecation, you changed the prompt, volume 3×.

Action: same set version (unless you must grow it), fill a new row on the table, inspect new failures, update the log, change the pin in one PR.

Shadow the new id at 5% if the risk is high. Do not 100% cutover on a Friday.

If quality holds and price dropped, take the win. If quality dropped 3 points, maybe stay on the old snapshot until you adapt the prompt — or stay forever if the pin still exists.

## Failure modes

1. **See you in prod.**

2. **Friday 100% cutover.**

3. **Assuming cheaper unit price** without token counts.

4. **No trigger** in the log.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

When the alias or the price moves I re-run the golden set, I fill a new table row, and I change the pin on purpose. I will not discover a snapshot change in production. If I cannot re-run I do not own the model.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Triggers: alias, price, deprecation, prompt, volume.
- Prove it in an artefact: Same set, new table row.
- Prove it in an artefact: Inspect new failures.
- Prove it in an artefact: Shadow if risky; no Friday 100%.
- Prove it in an artefact: Cheaper unit ≠ cheaper task.
- Prove it in an artefact: If you cannot re-run, you do not own it.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: When the alias or the price moves I re-run the golden set, I fill a new table row, and I change the pin on purpose. I will not discover a snapshot change in production. If I cannot re-run I do not own the model.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.q: The vendor changes the default alias. What do you do?
questions.a: Keep the pin. Run the golden set on the new id in shadow. Compare the table. Promote with a PR if it wins.

questions.q: Why might a cheaper unit price still cost more?
questions.a: The new snapshot is wordier or needs retries. Tokens per successful task can rise.

questions.q: Quality fell on a Monday and nobody shipped code. First check?
questions.a: Did an alias move? Re-run the set on the resolved snapshot.

questions.q: What belongs in the pin-change PR?
questions.a: The new table row, failure notes, and a rollback to the old id.

questions.q: When do you 100% cut over on a Friday?
questions.a: You do not. Shadow, then a weekday with people awake.
